items.title: Evolution Strategy-Based Calibration for Low-Bit Quantization of Speech Models
items.authors: Lucas RAKOTOARIVONY(Thales)
items.abstract: Quantization has become essential for the efficient deployment of speech processing systems. Although widely studied, most existing quantization methods were developed for vision and NLP architectures, while the specific challenges of audio signals remain largely overlooked. In particular, we show that audio activations can exhibit large calibration ranges, leading to significant information loss when standard calibration techniques are applied. To address this, we propose ESC, an Evolution Strategy-based Calibration method that formulates activation scaling as an optimization problem and solves it using a two-step local-global scheme driven by an evolution strategy. ESC enables unaltered performance under full INT8 quantization and is the first calibration method to achieve near-lossless performance for full INT4 quantization across multiple speech tasks. Integrating ESC with PTQ methods further reduces performance loss, achieving a 1% relative accuracy degradation on the AST model.

items.title: ProLAP: Probabilistic Language-Audio Pre-Training
items.authors: Toranosuke Manabe(Keio University); Yuchi Ishikawa(Keio University; LY Corporation); Hokuto Munakata(LY Corporation); Yoshimitsu Aoki(Keio University); Tatsuya Komatsu(LY Corporation)
items.abstract: Language-audio representation learning typically assumes one-to-one correspondence between audio and text. However, the relationship is inherently many-to-many: an audio segment can be described by multiple levels of specificity and vice versa. This oversimplification prevents models from learning the underlying data hierarchy. Unlike in vision-language domains, extending hierarchical modeling to audio is non-trivial due to complex sound source superposition. To address this, we propose Probabilistic Language-Audio Pre-training (ProLAP), representing inputs as probability distributions in a joint embedding space. For evaluation, we introduce two diagnostic datasets (AudioCaps-HC, AudioCaps-EC) for hierarchical analysis. Through a novel audio traversal task and inclusion tests, we demonstrate that ProLAP significantly outperforms deterministic baselines in capturing semantic hierarchy and yields intuitive uncertainty estimations, without sacrificing audio-text retrieval performance.

items.title: AdaTT: Text-Guided Instrument Timbre Transfer with Target-Adaptive Structural Control
items.authors: Dabin Kim(KAIST); Junwon Lee(KAIST); Juhan Nam(KAIST)
items.abstract: This paper addresses timbral ambiguity in instrument timbre transfer under fine-grained structural conditions. We argue this issue stems from instrument-specific expressive details in these conditions, which conflict with the target timbral properties. For example, imposing a violin's pitch-dominant vibrato contours onto a flute, which naturally exhibits loudness-dominant vibrato, impairs timbral fidelity. We propose AdaTT, a target-adaptive system that ensures high timbral fidelity across diverse timbre transfer scenarios within the ControlNet scheme. It selectively scales the frame-wise influence of pitch and loudness controls via text prompts to match the target instrument's identity. We also present a semi-automatic data construction pipeline to teach the model which expressive details to transform or preserve. Results show AdaTT achieves superior timbral fidelity and naturalness while retaining score-level content. Audio samples are available at https://dabinkim0. github.io/adatt/.

items.title: SARA: A Dual-Stream VAE for High-Fidelity Speech Generation via Integrating Semantic and Acoustic Representations
items.authors: Peijie Chen(Xiamen University); Wenhao Guan(Xiamen University); Weijie Wu(Xiamen University); Kaidi Wang(Xiamen University); Daiyu Huang(DiDi Global Inc.); Zhuanling Zha(DiDi Global Inc.); Junbo Li(DiDi Global Inc.); Jun Fang(DiDi Global Inc.); Qingyang Hong(Xiamen University); Lin Li(Xiamen University)
items.abstract: Zero-shot text-to-speech (TTS) relies on robust speech representations. However, current speech tokenizers face a fundamental trade-off: acoustic codecs preserve high-fidelity audio but lack linguistic constraints, causing content errors during generation, whereas semantic tokens from self-supervised learning (SSL) models ensure precise text alignment but discard some acoustic information. To bridge this gap, we propose SARA, a dual-stream VAE that directly fuses a frozen SSL semantic anchor with a dedicated residual acoustic encoder. This effectively mitigates the dilemma, creating an efficient and compact latent space without relying on complex regularizers. SARA achieves superior reconstruction quality over strong baselines. Furthermore, in downstream zero-shot TTS tasks, it yields highly natural and expressive synthesis quality, and maintains robust generation performance even under accelerated inference, offering a favorable trade-off between synthesis speed and computational cost.

items.title: BeatGain - A Rhythmic Pattern Enhancement Algorithm for Music Listening with Cochlear Implants
items.authors: Benjamin Lentz(Ruhr-Universität Bochum); Theresa Hartmann(Ruhr-Universität Bochum); Anil Nagathil(Ruhr-Universität Bochum); Ian Bruce(McMaster University); Rainer Martin(Ruhr-Universität Bochum)
items.abstract: Cochlear implants (CIs) enable speech understanding in individuals with profound hearing loss, yet music perception often remains limited. As CI users typically prefer music with a clear beat and reduced instrumental complexity, music enhancement strategies commonly emphasize vocals or percussive instruments. We propose a complementary approach that explicitly adapts to the rhythmic structure of a music signal. Percussive events aligned with the main beat are amplified, while weaker off-beat events are attenuated within a music mixing framework. Objective measures indicate reduced complexity compared to both the unprocessed signal and a baseline remixing approach. In a listening experiment, the proposed BeatGain method was significantly preferred over all reference conditions in terms of rhythmic clarity, and in all but one comparisons in terms of overall quality. These results support rhythm-focused processing as a promising extension of music enhancement methods for CI listeners.

items.title: Edit the Moment, Keep the Rest: Time-Localized Audio Editing via Instruction
items.authors: Jinwoo Jung(Hanyang University); Gihun Son(Hanyang University); Won-Gook Choi(Hanyang University); Joon-Hyuk Chang(Hanyang University)
items.abstract: Audio editing aims to modify sound content while maintaining its acoustic context. However, few studies have addressed temporal audio editing with precise control of event timing. We propose edit the moment, keep the rest (EMKR), an instruction-driven framework built on Stable Audio Open that supports adding, removing, replacing, moving, and extending. EMKR is trained with a temporal editing pipeline that constructs triplets (instruction, input audio, target audio), where the instruction carries information about when to edit. It further incorporates an explicit edit interval for precise timing and a source-event mask that preserves the original event instance in moving and extending. Experiments on mixtures from real-world datasets show that EMKR enables time-localized editing of polyphonic audio with 100 ms precision while preserving non-edited regions. This temporal control enables timing-critical editing tasks in polyphonic mixtures. Audio samples are available online.1

items.title: Repurposing a Speech Classifier for Guided Diffusion-Based Speech Generation
items.authors: Rostislav Makarov(University of Hamburg); Timo Gerkmann(University of Hamburg)
items.abstract: Classifier guidance is a way to control diffusion generation by using a noise-conditioned classifier to steer the sampling process toward a target class. One drawback of classifier guidance is that it requires two separately trained models: a classifier and a diffusion model. We therefore study a more compact alternative in which a conventionally trained speech classifier is repurposed as the backbone for diffusion generation. Starting from a frozen noise-conditioned classifier in log-Mel space, we attach a lightweight subnetwork that reuses intermediate classifier representations and train only this subnetwork under a Denoising Score Matching objective. Our work shows that a pretrained classifier can be repurposed for conditional generation, providing an appealing bridge between discriminative modeling and conditional speech synthesis resulting in high speech quality within a single-backbone model, with reduced memory footprint and computational cost.

items.title: Exploring Pre-training Benefits on Phoneme Addition through Fine-tuning in Speech Synthesis
items.authors: Masato Murata(CyberAgent; Nagoya University); Koichi Miyazaki(CyberAgent); Tomoki Koriyama(CyberAgent); Tomoki Toda(Nagoya University)
items.abstract: Transfer learning is widely used for low-resource text-to-speech. When the target corpus contains phonemes unseen in pre-training, the model must expand its phoneme inventory during fine-tuning; we call the process "phoneme addition." However, it remains unclear whether the pre-trained ability to generate seen phonemes contributes to this process. This study investigates phoneme addition in two settings: (1) a simulation setup using LLM-generated phoneme-controlled corpora that enables investigation without considering confounding factors, and (2) a real-speech cross-lingual transfer setup (English to Japanese) to validate whether the findings hold in practice. Experiments in both settings showed that while fine-tuning achieved higher naturalness than training from scratch, it required as much or more data to achieve comparable PER for new phonemes. These results indicate that pre-training mainly contributes to naturalness improvement, but offers limited benefit for phoneme addition.

items.title: ES-3DF: Editable Speech-Driven 3D Face Reconstruction via Geometry Texture Disentanglement
items.authors: Jianrong Wang(Tianjin University; Tianjin Renai College); Kaibin Bi(Tianjin University); Jinghui Li(Tianjin Renai College); Ju Zhang(Tianjin University of Technology); Qi Li(Tianjin University); Ying Guo(Tianjin University); Jing Zhao(Tianjin Beiyang Rongke Intelligent Technology Co., Ltd.)
items.abstract: Speech-driven facial generation typically relies on 2D synthesis, limiting realism and applicability. We propose ES-3DF, the first framework to reconstruct editable, textured 3D faces directly from speech. ES-3DF employs a Disentangle module that decouples facial features into 3DMM geometry and UV texture maps to enable fine-grained editing. To bridge the modality gap, we introduce a Dual-Branch Alignment module enhanced by a Class-Aware Multi-Slot Memory Bank. By leveraging a novel Multi-Slot InfoNCE loss, this mechanism dynamically aligns speech embeddings with diverse, evolving speaker prototypes, significantly improving identity preservation in the latent space. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ES-3DF outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in geometric accuracy, identity preservation, and visual quality, underscoring its potential for realistic 3D avatar generation.

items.title: K-DIALECT : Korean Dialect-Aware Face-Based Speech Synthesis
items.authors: Seongyeon Yang(Sungkyunkwan University); Juyeob Lee(Sungkyunkwan University); Eunil Park(Sungkyunkwan University; Jaume I University)
items.abstract: Korean exhibits substantial regional variation, comprising five major dialects in addition to the standard Seoul dialect. These dialects convey distinctive prosodic patterns and reflect important aspects of cultural and speaker identities. However, most Text-to-Speech (TTS) systems are primarily designed for standard language, limiting their ability to represent dialectal characteristics, particularly in low-resource dialect settings. Although face-based speech synthesis provides a viable alternative when reference audio is scarce or noisy, modeling dialectal prosody within this paradigm remains largely unexplored. To address this gap, we propose K-DIALECT, a multimodal face-based TTS framework for synthesizing low-resource Korean dialects. The model integrates a face encoder, a dialect-conditioned pitch predictor, and a FiLM-based fusion module. Experiments on six Korean dialects demonstrate improvements in dialectal fluency, naturalness, and modality alignment.

items.title: Feature Design and Generative Modelling in Deep Articulatory Synthesis
items.authors: Charles McGhee(University of Cambridge); Mark J.F. Gales(University of Cambridge); Kate M. Knill(University of Cambridge)
items.abstract: A deep articulatory synthesiser learns a mapping from a set of articulatory features to a set of acoustic features. A growing use case of articulatory synthesis is as an evaluation method for articulatory inversion, the process of estimating articulation from speech. To complete the loop from speech to articulation to speech, information lost during inversion must be added back in to faithfully recreate the input speech. This information can be added explicitly via additional input features or implicitly through generative modelling. However, by adding this information back into the synthesis process, the resulting speech may not be representative of the articulation estimated from inversion. In this work, we explore the impact of different feature inputs and modelling types on the output of a synthesiser, demonstrating that careful design choices are required to make claims about articulation through synthesis results.

items.title: From Tokens to Faces: Investigating Discrete Speech Representations for 3D Facial Animation
items.authors: Pedro R. Corrêa(UNICAMP; Univ. Grenoble Alpes, CNRS, Grenoble INP, GIPSA-lab); Olivier Perrotin(Univ. Grenoble Alpes, CNRS, Grenoble INP, GIPSA-lab); Samir Sadok(Inria at Univ. Grenoble Alpes); Paula D. P. Costa(UNICAMP); Thomas Hueber(Univ. Grenoble Alpes, CNRS, Grenoble INP, GIPSA-lab)
items.abstract: The choice of speech representation is critical in speech-driven 3D facial animation. Representations differ in what they encode: SSL features emphasize segmental and semantic cues, neural codecs yield latents optimized for acoustic reconstruction, and ASR-style objectives produce label-based spaces. We evaluate four speech representation families for 3D facial synthesis, comparing their facial reconstruction quality across two facial decoders using objective metrics and a perceptual evaluation. We additionally conduct probing analyses that relate tokenized representations to phonetic units and to articulatory deformations. We found that encoding phonetic classes is beneficial for accurate facial animation prediction on both semantic and label-based representations with comparable facial animation quality. From the latter, we introduce an Audio Visual Text-to-Speech (AVTTS) pipeline that leverages, as a shared space, discrete representations to decode speech and 3D facial motion.

items.title: Not Quite My Tempo: Voice Activity-aware Speech Synthesis for Lip-Synchronous Dubbing
items.authors: Alejandro Pérez-González-de-Martos(AppTek GmbH); Florian Lux(AppTek GmbH); Angelina Elizarova(AppTek GmbH); Milana Shkhanukova(AppTek GmbH); Andreas Kellner(AppTek GmbH); Mattia Antonino Di Gangi(AppTek GmbH)
items.abstract: Automatic lip-synchronous dubbing requires a speech synthesis model to generate alternating voice and silence patterns in the target language that match the timing of the source clip precisely to ensure an optimal viewing experience. Prior works address this problem by conditioning the speech synthesis process on lip movements extracted from the video signal. In this work, we condition the speech generation on a binary voice-activity signal, which has a lightweight representation and can be produced in multiple ways. We show that the model follows the voice-activity signal with high accuracy while maintaining natural prosody and semantically appropriate pause placement within sentences, as demonstrated through extensive objective and subjective evaluations. By randomly masking this condition during training, we make the feature entirely optional during inference, allowing editors to enforce or relax lip-sync constraints when desired.

items.title: GETS: Guiding EMG-to-Speech Synthesis via Silent Speech Recognition
items.authors: Jiwon Lee(Seoul National University); Jaejun Lee(Seoul National University); Kyogu Lee(Seoul National University)
items.abstract: Electromyography-to-speech (ETS) offers a promising solution for voicing silent speech, yet conventional methods often struggle to achieve high semantic intelligibility. We introduce GETS, a novel framework that establishes a new state-of-the-art (SOTA) with a Word Error Rate (WER) of 11.89% on the silent EMG test set. GETS comprises a diffusion-based generative network conditioned on EMG signals, integrated with a semantic guidance mechanism derived from silent speech recognition (SSR). Our framework not only demonstrates superior semantic intelligibility by effectively disambiguating underspecified EMG inputs but also faithfully preserves the prosodic characteristics--such as temporal alignment and energy contours--inherent in the original EMG signals. This synergistic fusion of acoustic EMG cues and SSR-based semantic guidance establishes a new benchmark for high-fidelity, naturalistic silent speech communication.

items.title: Enhancing EMG-to-Speech via Silent-Voiced Representation Alignment
items.authors: Jiwon Lee(Seoul National University); Injune Hwang(Seoul National University); Jaejun Lee(Seoul National University); Eungbeom Kim(Seoul National University); Dongyub Han(Seoul National University); Kyogu Lee(Seoul National University)
items.abstract: Silent Speech Interfaces (SSIs) offer an alternative communication pathway by reconstructing intelligible speech from non-acoustic biosignals such as facial electromyography (EMG). In particular, EMG can capture muscle activity associated with articulatory movements even in the absence of vocalization, serving as a suitable modality for silent speech synthesis. A major challenge in EMG-to-speech (ETS) research is the natural absence of ground-truth speech for silent EMG, along with the scarcity of available data. To address this, we propose a novel Silent-Voiced Alignment (SVA) loss, which introduces a multi-level representation-based alignment objective between utterance-parallel silent and voiced EMG pairs. Extensive experiments show that our method significantly enhances content reconstruction and can be seamlessly integrated into existing ETS frameworks. Furthermore, we demonstrate enhanced intelligibility and robustness under a standardized evaluation protocol.

items.title: Automatic pitch prediction from speech articulation: Where does the f0 information come from?
items.authors: Beliz Ozkan(Université Grenoble Alpes); Jonas Michael(Université Grenoble Alpes); Thomas Hueber(Université Grenoble Alpes); Olivier Perrotin(Université Grenoble Alpes)
items.abstract: While source-filter theory posits independence between the glottal source and vocal tract, empirical studies on silent speech interfaces predict fo from articulatory data. Using a multi-speaker dataset, we found that ultrasound tongue images alone do enable partial fo prediction. To resolve this paradox, we tested four hypotheses. We found no evidence that fo prediction (1) relies on a specific structure other than the tongue (or lips); (2) benefits from increased temporal context. However, (3) models trained on isolated utterances failed to generalise to spontaneous speech. Most importantly, (4) prominent words were predicted more accurately by capturing local correlations between fo and articulatory dynamics. These findings, corroborated by a perceptive experiment, highlight the need for realistic conversational training data and a focus on predicting local prosodic functions—rather than replicating global fo trajectories—to better capture the pragmatic role of fo in communication.

items.title: Speaker-Independent Speech Synthesis from Real-time MRI Articulatory Data
items.authors: Yuto Otani(Tokyo University of Science); Shun Sawada(Nippon Institute of Technology); Hidefumi Ohmura(Tokyo University of Science); Kouichi Katsurada(Tokyo University of Science)
items.abstract: This paper proposes a speaker-independent speech synthesis method that generates speech waveforms from real-time MRI (rtMRI) videos. The proposed model uses EfficientNetV2 for per-frame feature extraction, E-Branchformer for temporal modeling, and BigVGAN-v2 for speech synthesis. Speaker characteristics are acquired from rtMRI videos through cross-modal training with speaker embeddings, enabling speaker-independent synthesis from rtMRI videos alone. Experiments using the USC 75-Speaker Speech MRI Database demonstrate that the proposed method achieves favorable linguistic accuracy for read speech in a speaker-independent setting. F0 correlation analysis indicates that relative prosodic patterns are captured to a reasonable extent, as expected from visual articulatory information, though absolute F0 estimation remains challenging. Speaker similarity results show that although within-gender speaker discrimination proved difficult, speaker identity is reproduced to a reasonable degree.

items.title: From Dispersion to Attraction: Spectral Dynamics of Hallucination Across Whisper Model Scales
items.authors: Ivan Viakhirev(Mechanics and Optics University); Kirill Borodin(Moscow Technical University of Communications and Informatics; BitmanagerAI); Grach Mkrtchian(Moscow Technical University of Communications and Informatics)
items.abstract: Hallucinations in large ASR models present a critical safety risk. In this work, we propose the Spectral Sensitivity Theorem, which predicts a phase transition in deep networks from a dispersive regime (signal decay) to an attractor regime (rank-1 collapse) governed by layer-wise gain and alignment. We validate this theory by analyzing the eigenspectra of activation graphs in Whisper models (Tiny to Large-v3-Turbo) under adversarial stress. Our results are consistent with the theoretical prediction: intermediate models exhibit Structural Disintegration (Regime I), characterized by a 13.4% collapse in Cross-Attention rank. Conversely, large models enter a Compression-Seeking Attractor state (Regime II), where Self-Attention actively compresses rank (-2.34%) and hardens the spectral slope, decoupling the model from acoustic evidence.

items.title: Error Diversity and Performance Variability in Zero-Shot Children's Speech Recognition
items.authors: Abhijit Sinha(NIT Sikkim); Hemant Kumar Kathania(NIT Sikkim); Paban Sapkota(NIT Sikkim); Mikko Kurimo(Aalto University)
items.abstract: Children's speech recognition remains challenging due to acoustic variability and limited labeled data. This study analyzes the behavior of self-supervised learning (SSL) representations for children's speech recognition under a strict zero-shot adult-to-child transfer setting. Layer-wise representations from Wav2Vec2, HuBERT, and Data2Vec are evaluated using hybrid ASR systems trained only on adult speech. Although several layers achieve comparable best-case word error rates, substantial variability exists across representations. Error analysis reveals dataset-dependent error structures, while LLM-based post-recognition correction provides little improvement. Oracle analysis further shows that different layers capture complementary acoustic information, particularly under stronger domain mismatch. These findings indicate that recognition errors are primarily driven by acoustic representation limitations rather than recoverable linguistic inconsistencies.

items.title: Gender Bias in ASR: A Controlled Study of Gender Composition Across Training Paradigms
items.authors: Seshan S(Indian Institute of Science); Murali Kadambi(Indian Institute of Science); Amartya Veer(Indian Institute of Science); Prasanta Kumar Ghosh(Indian Institute of Science)
items.abstract: Gender disparities in ASR are commonly attributed to training data imbalance, often evaluated by fine-tuning pretrained systems on gender-controlled splits. We test whether such fine-tuning reveals a systematic relationship between training composition and gender disparity. Across three pretrained models and 11 splits spanning 0-100% female representation, male and female WERs fluctuate without consistent direction, yielding no systematic composition-disparity relationship. To determine whether the effect exists, we include a from-scratch system as a controlled reference under identical conditions. In contrast, this system exhibits consistent, directional disparity shifts as composition varies, confirming that the effect is real but masked in pretrained models by representations established during large-scale pretraining. These results demonstrate that balancing fine-tuning data alone is insufficient to mitigate gender disparity in pretrained ASR.

items.title: Balancing ASR and diarization in end-to-end LLMs for multi-talker speech recognition
items.authors: Naijun Zheng(Huawei); Yuke Lin(Huawei); Sanli Tian(Huawei); Mengtian Li(Huawei); Zhiwei Lin(Huawei); Longshuai Xiao(Huawei); Dandan Tu(Huawei)
items.abstract: Multi-talker speech recognition is often addressed by combining automatic speech recognition (ASR) and speaker diarization in a pipeline system. Recently, LLM-based approaches have shown promise by jointly modeling semantic and speaker information, but they typically require large-scale multi-talker corpora that are costly to annotate. In this paper, we investigate how to efficiently train an LLM-based system with limited real-recorded data while maintaining high accuracy in speaker attribution. We propose several strategies: (1) a dual-encoder architecture to extract semantic and speaker features, (2) a feature interleaving format to merge these features as the inputs to the LLM, (3) a length-aware speaker ID loss to enhance diarization capability, and (4) an adaptive threshold strategy for ASR loss computation to mitigate hallucinations caused by speech overlaps. These strategies balance training between ASR and diarization tasks. Our system outperforms open-source baseline approaches, achieving relative improvements of 18% on the Al-iMeeting corpus and 24% on the Aishell4 corpus.

items.title: Multi-Talker ASR Unaffected by Speaker Change Count
items.authors: Naoki Makishima(NTT, Inc.); Suzuka Yamada(NTT, Inc.); Taiga Yamane(NTT, Inc.); Mana Ihori(NTT, Inc.); Tanaka Tomohiro(NTT, Inc.); Satoshi Suzuki(NTT, Inc.); Shota Orihashi(NTT, Inc.); Ryo Masumura(NTT, Inc.)
items.abstract: We develop an autoregressive model for multi-talker automatic speech recognition (ASR) robust to the number of speaker changes. Recent studies on multi-talker ASR handle multiple speakers by recursively estimating a single token sequence formed by concatenating their transcripts with speaker change tokens. However, as this technique heavily relies on context including speaker change tokens, inference performance degrades when the number of speaker changes exceeds those in the training data. To address this limitation, we estimate the token sequence, including speaker change tokens, without relying on how many speaker changes have occurred. This is achieved by introducing a novel speaker change token mask in self-attention, which sets the values of speaker change tokens and randomly selected tokens referenced by other queries to zero, preventing the model from inferring the number of speaker changes from context. Experiments demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method.

items.title: WildElder: A Chinese Elderly Speech Dataset from the Wild with Fine-Grained Manual Annotations
items.authors: Hui Wang(Nankai University); Jiaming Zhou(Nankai University); Jiabei He(Nankai University); Haoqin Sun(Nankai University); Yong Qin(Nankai University)
items.abstract: Elderly speech poses unique challenges for automatic processing due to age-related changes such as slower articulation and vocal tremors. Existing Chinese datasets are mostly recorded in controlled environments, limiting their diversity and real-world applicability. To address this gap, we present WildElder, a Mandarin elderly speech corpus collected from online videos and enriched with fine-grained manual annotations, including transcription, speaker age, gender, and accent strength. Combining the realism of in-the-wild data with expert curation, WildElder enables robust research on automatic speech recognition and speaker profiling. Experimental results reveal both the difficulties of elderly speech recognition and the potential of WildElder as a challenging new benchmark. The dataset and code have been available at https://github.com/NKU-HLT/WildElder.

items.title: Post-ASR Proper Noun Grounding via Multi-View Phonetic and Semantic Retrieval
items.authors: Pranshu Nema(Augnito India Private Limited); Kush Shrivastava(Augnito India Private Limited); Bhavik Vachhani(Augnito India Private Limited); Rustom Lawyer(Augnito India Private Limited)
items.abstract: Modern end-to-end automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems achieve strong overall transcription accuracy but remain vulnerable to proper nouns and long-tail vocabulary. Such errors are often phonetically plausible yet lexically incorrect, degrading downstream systems that rely on accurate entity interpretation. We propose a post-ASR proper noun grounding framework that links noisy mentions to ranked candidates from a predefined lexicon without retraining or modifying the ASR model. The method integrates complementary similarity views: fine-grained phonetic representations via grapheme-to-phoneme (G2P), coarse phonetic encoding using Soundex, and context-aware semantic embeddings, with normalized score fusion for unified ranking. Multi-view fusion increases Recall@1 over vanilla exact match by 36.4 and 23.6 percentage points for Whisper-large-v3 and Qwen3-ASR-1.7B, reaching 74.67% and 59.82% respectively, with up to 87.36% Recall@10 in the strongest configuration.

items.title: From Text Metrics to Model Internals: A Study of Whisper ASR Hallucination Detection
items.authors: Jan Jasiński(AGH University of Krakow); Mateusz Barański(AGH University of Krakow); Julitta Bartolewska(AGH University of Krakow); Marcin Witkowski(AGH University of Krakow); Konrad Kowalczyk(AGH University of Krakow)
items.abstract: Hallucinations of ASR models — fluent transcriptions with no basis in audio — degrade system performance and pose risks in downstream applications. Robust detection of such errors remains a challenge. This paper studies Whisper large v3 hallucination detection on real-speech human-annotated data across three paradigms: text-based, LLM-based, and internal decoder state probing. Text classifiers utilizing metrics for text evaluation achieve high recall but degrade without reference transcripts. LLM-based detection improves precision with domain-specific prompt conditioning, yet remains less competitive than the lightweight text-based methods. Probing Whisper's decoder representations, without a ground-truth reference, yields the strongest performance, revealing that hallucination traits are encoded across intermediate decoding layers. A late-fusion meta-classifier combining text and internal-state outputs achieves the best overall detection performance.

items.title: Grounding Whisper: An Audio Anchor-Based Approach for Hallucination Mitigation and Throughput-Efficient ASR
items.authors: Prateek Agarwal(Walmart Global Tech); Saurabh Kumar(Walmart Global Tech); Priyanka Bhatt(Walmart Global Tech)
items.abstract: Whisper exhibits robust ASR performance but suffers from hallucinations on silence and non-speech audio, generating spurious transcriptions that undermine production reliability. We introduce anchor audio, a simple input-level technique that prepends a short audio phrase with near-zero domain occurrence to the input, enabling hallucination detection without modifying or fine-tuning the model. Using this mechanism, we evaluate five inference approaches ranging from single-call augmentation to batch concatenation with automatic fallback, exploring accuracy-latency-throughput trade-offs. Our batch strategy leverages Whisper's fixed 30-second window to concatenate multiple short utterances while maintaining fidelity through anchor-based validation. This reduces overall WER from 32.18% to 13.23%, achieves 0.14% Hallucination Error Rate on non-speech audio, and preserves latency comparable to baseline VAD pipelines, demonstrating an effective, practical solution for hallucination mitigation.

items.title: Convolutional Dynamic Rotary Positional Encoding
items.authors: Euijin Hong(Carnegie Mellon University); Mengchun Zhang(University of Pittsburgh)
items.abstract: Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) is a strong alternative to relative positional encoding in modern automatic speech recognition (ASR) encoder models. However, its discrete, uniformly-spaced chronological index is misaligned with the continuous, semantic nature of speech features. We propose Convolutional Dynamic RoPE (CD-RoPE), a dynamic positional encoding complementing Branchformer's attention path by warping the rotary temporal index conditioned on local acoustic context via a lightweight depthwise-separable convolution. Additive position modulation preserves RoPE's harmonic structure, enabling continuous input-dependent shifts. CD-RoPE achieves consistent WER improvements over RelPos on Branchformer across all LibriSpeech test sets with 2.2M fewer parameters. Targeted robustness evaluation on Speech Robust Bench (SRB) confirms that CD-RoPE's advantage is strongest under temporal perturbations, validating the temporal warping mechanism.

items.title: Diffusion Language Models for Speech Recognition
items.authors: Davyd Naveriani(RWTH Aachen University); Albert Zeyer(RWTH Aachen University; AppTek); Ralf Schlüter(RWTH Aachen University; AppTek); Hermann Ney(RWTH Aachen University; AppTek)
items.abstract: Diffusion language models have recently emerged as a leading alternative to standard language models, due to their ability for bidirectional attention and parallel text generation. In this work, we explore variants for their use in speech recognition. Specifically, we introduce a comprehensive guide to incorporating masked diffusion language models (MDLM) and uniform-state diffusion models (USDMs) for rescoring ASR hypotheses. Additionally, we designed a new joint-decoding method that combines CTC and USDM by integrating the framewise probability distributions derived from CTC with the labelwise probability distributions computed by USDM at each decoding step, thereby generating new candidates that combine strong language knowledge from USDM and acoustic information from CTC. Our findings reveal that USDM, as well as MDLM, can significantly improve the accuracy of recognised text. We publish all our code and recipes.

items.title: Do speech foundation models really learn words?
items.authors: Robin Huo(University of Toronto); Ewan Dunbar(University of Toronto)
items.abstract: Self-supervised speech foundation models are now used in a wide array of downstream applications, including traditional speech recognition and as the basis for tokens in speech-aware language models. Attempts to understand their usefulness have largely focused on probing their representations' ability to discriminate phonemes and words. However, discriminative ability for words need not imply specialized representation of words per se. Good discrimination of words may be explained by good encoding of word form (phonemes) rather than form-independent word representations encoding identity or syntactic/semantic properties. By partialling out phoneme information using residualization, we show that, in later layers, HuBERT and wav2vec 2.0 do in general learn representations which encode words with reasonable fidelity independently of local phonetic content. We show that this simple approach to disentanglement can enhance higher-order linguistic information in word discovery tasks.

items.title: Readability Does Not Predict Speech Recognition Errors: Contrasting Human and Machine Perception.
items.authors: Baptiste Ramonda(IRIT, CNRS, UT; QUT); Laurianne Sitbon(QUT); Julien Pinquier(IRIT, CNRS, UT)
items.abstract: This study challenges the historical link between the readability of a text and its intelligibility by automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems. While textual complexity has a significant impact on human comprehension, its effect on modern end-to-end architectures remains unclear. We present a controlled experimental pipeline using the CLEAR corpus, speech synthesis, and acoustic degradations (babble noise, reverberation). Our results demonstrate a near-perfect decoupling between readability, measured by the Global Readability Index, and intelligibility, measured by the Word Error Rate. This orthogonality persists under different acoustic degradations and is validated on natural speech. The absence of a "cognitive load" on the model during the transcription process confirms that it is now completely independent of textual complexity.

items.title: Probing Linguistic Information in Speech Embeddings: A Diagnostic Analysis across Acoustic and Structural Domains
items.authors: Simon Gonzalez(DSTG); Tao Hoang(DSTG); Hayden Ooi(DSTG); Chloe Dean(DSTG); Bradley Donnelly(DSTG); Myung Kim(DSTG); Latchman Singh(DSTG); Jason Littlefield(DSTG); Tim Cawley(DSTG); Jennifer Biggs(DSTG)
items.abstract: Speech embeddings have become a central component of modern automatic speech recognition and speech-language models; however, their linguistic interpretability is still under active research. This study adopts a diagnostic approach to examine the extent to which speech embeddings encode linguistic features. We analyse linear associations between pretrained acoustic embeddings and a set of core acoustic, phonetic, and linguistic structure features. The results show that embeddings encode acoustic and phonetic properties, particularly temporal dynamics, spectral structure, and voice-quality related features, while higher-level linguistic structure is represented more weakly. Lexical complexity shows a measurable association, whereas morphological and syntactic complexity show limited linear accessibility. These findings suggest that embeddings capture linguistic information in a distributed and gradient manner, with strongest sensitivity to properties closely tied to signal realisation.

items.title: I Am No One: Style-Aware Paraphrasing for Text Anonymization
items.authors: Ahmed Sohair Khan(RMIT University); Estrid He(RMIT University); Monica Wachowicz(RMIT University); Elham Naghizade(RMIT University)
items.abstract: Authorship attribution models can re-identify users from seemingly anonymized text by exploiting stable stylistic fingerprints, even after explicit identifiers are removed, posing a growing privacy risk for text publishing and analytics. This risk extends to speech-derived text such as ASR transcripts of meetings and call-center conversations, where stylometric leakage can persist even after acoustic anonymization. Differential privacy-based anonymization often severely degrades text quality and utility. We propose a style-aware, prompt-driven anonymization approach that uses pretrained large language models to construct compact stylistic profiles from minimal samples and rewrite text to suppress identifiable style markers while preserving meaning. Across blog and review datasets, our approach reduces authorship attribution F1 by 60-70% while maintaining content quality and readability, substantially outperforming DP-based and non-DP baselines.

title: Spoken Language Understanding
header: Wednesday 30 September 2026 - 16:30-18:30 - Area 11 - Poster 1 - Spoken Language Understanding

items.title: DEBATE: A Dataset for Disentangling Textual Ambiguity in Mandarin Through Speech
items.authors: Haotian Guo(Hunan University); Jing Han(Hunan University; Yuelushan Center for Industrial Innovation); Yongfeng Tu(Malanshan Audio & Video Laboratory); Shihao Gao(Hunan University); Weihao Gan(Malanshan Audio & Video Laboratory); Zixing Zhang(Hunan University)
items.abstract: Despite extensive research on textual and visual disambiguation, disambiguation through speech (DTS) remains underexplored. This is largely due to the lack of high-quality datasets that pair spoken sentences with richly ambiguous text. To address this gap, we present DEBATE, a unique public Chinese speech-text dataset designed to study how speech cues and patterns such as pronunciation, pauses, stress, and intonation can help resolve textual ambiguity and reveal a speaker's true intent. DEBATE contains 1,001 carefully selected ambiguous utterances, each recorded by 10 native speakers to capture diverse spoken disambiguations. We detail the rigorous data pipeline and benchmark threelarge speech language models, revealing a significant gap between machine and human intent understanding. DEBATE represents the first effort of its kind and offers a foundation for building similar DTS datasets across languages and cultures.

items.title: Distilling Structured Reasoning into SpeechLLMs for Spoken Language Understanding
items.authors: Toshihiro Tsukagoshi(Shizuoka University); Natsuo Yamashita(Hitachi, Ltd.); Kota Dohi(Hitachi, Ltd.); Hiroaki Kokubo(Hitachi, Ltd.); Masaaki Yamamoto(Hitachi, Ltd.)
items.abstract: Recent Speech Large Language Models (SpeechLLMs) have emerged as a promising approach for end-to-end Spoken Language Understanding (SLU). While adapting SpeechLLMs to specific SLU tasks such as intent classification requires alignment with task-specific label schemas, conventional fine-tuning still struggles to separate semantically adjacent intent categories. To address this, we propose Reasoning-Guided Fine-Tuning (RG-FT), which distills structured reasoning trajectories generated by DeepSeek-R1, comprising candidate enumeration, rejection reasoning, and label prediction, into SpeechLLMs as a multitask objective. Explicitly verbalizing why incorrect candidates are rejected forces the model to capture fine-grained distinctions and sharpen inter-class decision boundaries. At inference, only direct label prediction is used, incurring zero additional computational cost. Experiments on multiple SLU benchmarks and six SpeechLLMs demonstrate that RG-FT consistently improves SLU performance.

items.title: Enhancing Audio Reasoning via Semantic Summary Prediction
items.authors: Francesco Bonzi(Concordia University; Mila - Quebec AI Institute); Pooneh Mousavi(Concordia University; Mila - Quebec AI Institute); Cem Subakan(Université Laval; Mila - Quebec AI Institute); Mirco Ravanelli(Concordia University; Mila - Quebec AI Institute)
items.abstract: Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) perform well on complex question answering but often show a reasoning gap, where explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reduces accuracy compared to direct answers. We hypothesize that long reasoning sequences shift attention away from the audio input. To address this, we propose SPARE (Semantic Prediction for Audio REasoning), which introduces a register token aligned with the final conclusion using a cosine similarity loss with a Sentence-BERT embedding. This conditions the model's latent space with the target semantic goal before reasoning begins. Experiments on MMAU and MMAR with SALMONN show improved zero-shot reasoning and stronger early attention to audio without additional inference cost.

items.title: Incremental End-to-End Spoken Dialogue State Tracking with a Multimodal LLM and Reinforcement Learning
items.authors: Tomoya Higuchi(The University of Electro-Communications); Michimasa Inaba(The University of Electro-Communications)
items.abstract: End-to-end spoken dialogue state tracking (DST) infers belief states directly from speech, avoiding cascading errors in ASR-DST pipelines. This paper proposes an incremental DST method using a multimodal large language model (Qwen2.5-Omni-7B) that generates transcripts and symbolic state updates from raw audio. Unlike conventional approaches that regenerate the full state each turn, our method predicts only symbolic edit operations relative to the previous state, reducing output length and the risk of corrupting unchanged slots. We apply a two-stage training recipe: supervised fine-tuning followed by Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), which directly optimizes generation-level rewards for transcript accuracy, DST correctness, and format validity. Experiments on SpokenWOZ demonstrate that incremental updates substantially outperform full-state prediction, and GRPO further improves accuracy, achieving the best reported results on this benchmark.

items.title: Joint Speech And Text Training For LLM-based End-To-End Spoken Dialogue State Tracking
items.authors: Katia Vendrame(Brno University of Technology); Bolaji Yusuf(Brno University of Technology); Santosh Kesiraju(Brno University of Technology); Šimon Sedláček(Brno University of Technology); Oldřich Plchot(Brno University of Technology); Honza Černocký(Brno University of Technology)
items.abstract: End-to-end spoken dialogue state tracking (DST) is made difficult by having to handle speech input with scarce training data. Combining speech foundation encoders and large language models has emerged as an approach to alleviate this difficulty. Although this approach results in strong spoken DST models, achieving state-of-the-art performance in realistic multi-turn DST, it struggles to generalize across domains and requires annotated spoken DST training data for each domain of interest. However, collecting such data for every target domain is both costly and difficult. Noting that textual DST data is more easily obtained for various domains, in this work, we propose jointly training on available spoken DST data and written textual data from other domains as a way to achieve cross-domain generalization. We conduct experiments which show the efficacy of our proposed method for getting good cross-domain DST performance without relying on spoken training data from the target domains.

items.title: MAC-SLU: Multi-Intent Automotive Cabin Spoken Language Understanding Benchmark
items.authors: Yuezhang Peng(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Chonghao Cai(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Ziang Liu(Central South University); Shuai Fan(AISpeech Co., Ltd.); Sheng Jiang(AISpeech Co., Ltd.); Hua Xu(AISpeech Co., Ltd.); Yuxin Liu(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Sheng Wang(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Qiguang Chen(Harbin Institute of Technology); Yao Li(Shanghai Aviation Electric Co., Ltd.); Kele Xu(National University of Defense Technology); Kai Yu(Shanghai Jiao Tong University; AISpeech Co., Ltd.); Libo Qin(Harbin Institute of Technology); Xie Chen(Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Shanghai Innovation Institute)
items.abstract: Spoken Language Understanding (SLU), which aims to extract user semantics for downstream tasks, is vital to task-oriented dialog systems. Existing SLU datasets generally lack diversity and complexity, and a unified benchmark for the latest Large Language Models (LLMs) and Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) remains absent. This work introduces MAC-SLU, a novel Multi-Intent Automotive Cabin Spoken Language Understanding Dataset, which increases task difficulty with authentic and complex multi-intent data. Based on MAC-SLU, we benchmarked leading LLMs and LALMs, covering methods like in-context learning (ICL), supervised fine-tuning (SFT), as well as end-to-end (E2E) and pipeline paradigms. Experiments show that while LLMs and LALMs have the potential to complete SLU tasks through ICL, their performance still lags significantly behind SFT. Meanwhile, E2E LALMs demonstrate performance comparable to pipeline approaches and effectively avoid error propagation from speech recognition.

items.title: MSU-Bench: Towards Understanding the Conversational Multi-Speaker Scenarios
items.authors: Zhaokai Sun(ASLP@NPU; SZ Loop Area Inst.; Li Auto); Shuai Wang(Nanjing Univ.; SZ Loop Area Inst.); Zhennan Lin(ASLP@NPU); Chengyou Wang(ASLP@NPU); Dehui Gao(ASLP@NPU); Yuang Cao(ASLP@NPU); Chunjiang He(ASLP@NPU); Pan Zhou(Li Auto); Lei Xie(ASLP@NPU)
items.abstract: Spoken Language Understanding (SLU) is moving from task-specific pipelines toward large audio language models (LALMs) that generate natural-language responses. However, existing speech benchmarks mainly focus on single-speaker settings or isolated subtasks, leaving speaker-centric understanding in realistic multi-speaker conversations insufficiently evaluated. We introduce MSU-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark for multi-speaker conversational understanding, covering 16 speaker-centric tasks and 2,300 QA instances in a two-tier framework from speaker grounding to dialogue reasoning. We build a Gemini-assisted annotation and QA generation pipeline with human-in-the-loop verification, achieving high QA validity and strong agreement between human answers and verified labels. We further analyze speaker-referencing schemes and diagnostic error types to reveal bottlenecks in speaker grounding and reasoning. Experiments reveal clear gaps across model families, with closed-source systems leading overall but all models still facing challenges in complex speaker grounding and multi-speaker reasoning. The benchmark annotations, metadata, and evaluation scripts are available at the official GitHub repository: ASLP-lab/MSU-Bench.

items.title: MVCL-DAF++: Enhancing Multimodal Intent Recognition via Prototype-Aware Contrastive Alignment and Coarse-to-Fine Dynamic Attention Fusion
items.authors: Haofeng Huang(University of Shanghai for Science and Technology); Bin Li(CAS); Yifei Han(CAS); Long Zhang(CAS); Yangfan He(University of Minnesota-Twin Cities); Yaxin Xue(University of Leeds)
items.abstract: Multimodal intent recognition (MMIR) suffers from weak semantic grounding and poor robustness under noisy or rare-class conditions. We propose MVCL-DAF++, which extends MVCL-DAF with two key modules: (1) Prototype-aware contrastive alignment, aligning instances to class-level prototypes to enhance semantic consistency; and (2) Coarse-to-fine attention fusion, integrating global modality summaries with token-level features for hierarchical cross-modal interaction. On MIntRec and MIntRec2.0, MVCL-DAF++ achieves new state-of-the-art results, improving rare-class recognition by +1.05% and +4.18% WF1, respectively. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of prototype-guided learning and coarse-to-fine fusion for robust multimodal understanding.

items.title: PROGRESS: Coverage-guided RL to Train Search-augmented LLM Agent
items.authors: Sudipta Paul(Samsung Electronics); Vijay Srinivasan(Samsung Electronics); Vivek Kulkarni(Samsung Electronics); Aounon Kumar(Samsung Electronics); Yashas Malur Saidutta(Samsung Electronics); Wenbo Li(Samsung Electronics); Srinivas Chappidi(Samsung Electronics)
items.abstract: Existing search-augmented LLM agents are trained using Reinforcement Learning to boost its reasoning capabilities. However, these approaches primarily rely on outcome-level rewards which provide little supervision over search behavior and overlook agent's ability to decompose complex queries properly. To mitigate this issue, we propose PROGRESS which utilizes teacher-guided coverage reward to explicitly shape decomposed query generation of the policy model. During training, frozen teacher models are used to decompose complex queries into essential search queries. These essential search queries are utilized to guide the search behavior of the policy model. Integrated into an R1-style training framework, our approach provides lightweight guidance over query decomposition decisions without dense process-level supervision. Experiments show that coverage-guided RL improves overall task performance, highlighting the importance of explicitly supervising search strategies in agentic LLMs.

items.title: SFL-MTSC: Leveraging Semantic Frame-Level Multi-Task Self-Consistency for Robust Multi-Intent Spoken Language Understanding
items.authors: Po-Yen Chen(National Taiwan Normal University); Berlin Chen(National Taiwan Normal University)
items.abstract: Prompt-based spoken language understanding (SLU) with large language models (LLMs) often suffers from inconsistent intent-slot structures due to decoding stochasticity, particularly in multi-intent scenarios. In view of this, we propose Semantic Frame-Level Multi-Task Self-Consistency (SFL-MTSC), a novel structured aggregation framework operating at the semantic frame level. Instead of output-level majority voting, SFL-MTSC decomposes predictions into intent-specific frames, applies domain-intent grouping and slot-level clustering, and evaluates cluster reliability using path support scoring. Reliable frames are retained and re-integrated to form the final prediction. Zero-shot experiments on the MAC-SLU benchmark dataset show improved slot F1 and overall accuracy over single-path inference, while intent accuracy remains largely stable across most settings.

items.title: Selective Capability Unlearning in End-to-End Spoken Language Understanding
items.authors: Akanksha Singh(IISER Bhopal); Vinod Kumar Kurmi(IISER Bhopal)
items.abstract: Modern spoken language understanding (SLU) systems are increasingly deployed in real-world settings, where specific functionalities may need to be removed due to policy or safety constraints. In SLU, a functionality corresponds to an intent and its associated slot-generation behavior. However, in autoregressive models, suppressing a target intent does not eliminate the conditional mapping that generates slots conditioned on that intent. When the intent prefix is externally supplied, the model can reconstruct the original intent-slot structure. We identify this structural failure as capability persistence. We propose Binding Subspace (BSU), a representation-level framework that isolates and attenuates intent-conditioned directions underlying this mapping. Across SLU benchmarks, BSU substantially reduces forced-prefix recoverability while preserving retained performance.

items.title: GigaChat Audio: Time-aware Large Audio Language Model
items.authors: Aleksandr Kutsakov(SaluteDevices); Mariia Sadovina(SaluteDevices); Georgii Gospodinov(SaluteDevices); Alexandr Maximenko(SaluteDevices); Oleg Kutuzov(SaluteDevices); Pavel Bogomolov(SaluteDevices); Fyodor Minkin(SaluteDevices)
items.abstract: Temporal grounding in long recordings remains challenging for audio-conditioned LLMs. We present a time-aware audio LLM that answers questions with explicit timestamps over up to 120 minutes of input. Our approach interleaves periodic time markers with continuous audio tokens using large-scale synthetic supervision from a cascaded pipeline. Our model achieves strong temporal-grounding accuracy on short and long benchmarks and supports time-anchored fragment descriptions and summaries. Extensive ablations examine how time representation, marker frequency, tokenization, and duration-mixture design affect accuracy and computational cost. We release model weights and datasets to support further research on time-aware audio understanding, available at https://huggingface.co/ai-sage/GigaChat3.1-Audio-10B-A1.8B.

items.title: Multi-Phonation Graph Learning with Self-Supervised Speech Embeddings for ALS Detection and Progression Prediction
items.authors: Behrad TaghiBeyglou(Huawei Canada; University of Toronto); Fatemeh Bagheri(University of Toronto; North York General Hospital); Ervin Sejdic(University of Toronto; North York General Hospital)
items.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) progressively impairs speech motor control, making acoustic analysis a promising biomarker for severity and progression estimation. We propose a subject-level graph framework that aggregates multiple phonation recordings into a unique k-nearest-neighbor graph built from pretrained SSL embeddings of 2s segments. We compare four SSL front-ends (wav2vec 2.0, HuBERT, data2vec-audio, and UniSpeech-SAT) and five graph neural networks (GCN, residual GCN, GAT, GraphSAGE, and GIN) on the SAND dataset tasks (339 participants: 205 ALS, 134 control): 5-class dysarthria severity and 4-class ALSFRS-R progression prediction. On the official validation set, the best configuration (HuBERT+GIN) achieves macro-F1 of 0.73 for Task 1 and 0.69 for Task 2, outperforming SAND validation baselines (0.61 and 0.58). These results highlight the potential of combining GNNs with pretrained cross-lingual speech representations for low-resource ALS detection and progression monitoring.

items.title: Synthetic Pathological Speech at Scale: A Flow Matching Approach for Clinical Data Augmentation
items.authors: Alkis Koudounas(Sony Group Corporation); Moreno La Quatra(Kore University of Enna); Quentin Jodelet(Sony Group Corporation); Hayato Futami(Sony Group Corporation); Valerio Mario Salerno(Kore University of Enna); Sabato Marco Siniscalchi(Università degli Studi di Palermo); Emiru Tsunoo(Sony Group Corporation)
items.abstract: Deep learning for pathological voice detection suffers from severe data scarcity. Traditional augmentation often fails to capture the non-linear glottal instabilities of voice disorders. We propose a flow-based generative framework to synthesize pathological and healthy vowel phonations using clinical status token conditioning. We investigate scaling laws by training supervised classifiers on synthetic datasets ranging from 100 to 100,000 samples. Experiments across four languages show that classifiers trained solely on 100k synthetic samples surpass real-only baselines by +3.9% accuracy and +13.3% sensitivity on held-out real data. Synthetic augmentation further improves zero-shot transfer across multiple datasets on multi-class pathology classification (+7.4%/+10.0% F1) and Parkinson's detection from vowels (+6.8% accuracy). Our findings demonstrate that flow-based generative scaling effectively addresses data scarcity while improving cross-domain robustness.

items.title: Learning to Attend to Depression-Related Patterns: An Adaptive Cross-Modal Gating Network for Depression Detection
items.authors: Hangbin Yu(Shenzhen InstChinese Academy of Science; University of Chinese Academy of Sciences; State Key Laboratory of Biomedical Imaging Science and System); Yudong Yang(ShenzChinese Academy of Sciences; State Key Laboratory of Biomedical Imaging Science and System); Rongfeng Su(Chinese Academy of Sciences; State Key Laboratory of Biomedical Imaging Science and System); Nan Yan(Chinese Academy of Sciences; State Key Laboratory of Biomedical Imaging Science and System); Lan Wang(Shenzhen Institute of Advanced Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences; State Key Laboratory of Biomedical Imaging Science and System)
items.abstract: Automatic depression detection using speech signals with acoustic and textual modalities is a promising approach for early diagnosis. Depression-related patterns exhibit sparsity in speech: diagnostically relevant features occur in specific segments rather than being uniformly distributed. However, most existing methods treat all frames equally, assuming depression-related information is uniformly distributed and thus overlooking this sparsity. To address this issue, we propose a depression detection network based on Adaptive Cross-Modal Gating (ACMG) that adaptively reassigns frame-level weights across both modalities, enabling selective attention to depression-related segments. Experimental results show that the depression detection system with ACMG outperforms baselines without it. Visualization analyses further confirm that ACMG automatically attends to clinically meaningful patterns, including low-energy acoustic segments and textual segments containing negative sentiments.

items.title: Layer-wise Multi-factor Adaptive Disentanglement for Cross-corpus Speech Depression Detection
items.authors: Minggang Wang(Nagoya Institute of Technology; University of Wollongong); Shohei Kato(Nagoya Institute of Technology); Wen Gu(Nagoya Institute of Technology); Fenghui Ren(University of Wollongong); Jun Yan(University of Wollongong)
items.abstract: Although speaker disentanglement can improve within-corpus depression detection, cross-corpus transfer remains challenging as multi-source factor shifts are encoded and accumulated across the network hierarchy, making speaker-only and output-level constraints insufficient. To address this issue, we propose a Layer-wise Multi-factor Adaptive Disentanglement framework (LMAD) that enforces constraints at multiple key encoder layers to reduce the dependence of intermediate representations on speaker and corpus factors while preserving dependence on depression information, thereby mitigating the accumulation of nuisance information across layers. Furthermore, LMAD employs adaptive weights to modulate disentanglement strength along inter-layer and intra-layer dimensions. Experimental results shown that LMAD consistently outperforms both the baseline and speaker-only disentanglement models under bidirectional DAIC-WoZ↔Androids transfer, while maintaining competitive within-corpus performance.

items.title: Augmenting Dysarthric Speech Severity Assessment with MOS Supervision
items.authors: Kaimeng Jia(Tsinghua University); Minzhu Tu(Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications); Zengrui Jin(Tsinghua University); Siyin Wang(Tsinghua University); Chao Zhang(Tsinghua University)
items.abstract: Dysarthria is a speech disorder marked by reduced intelligibility and communicative effectiveness. Automatic utterance-level assessment of dysarthric speech can support scalable speech monitoring and therapy-related analysis. Yet training such systems is bottlenecked by the scarcity of clinically annotated dysarthric speech. This work proposes to augment dysarthric speech assessment using data from speech synthesis evaluations, specifically human-annotated utterances with Mean Opinion Score (MOS) labels from the QualiSpeech corpus. Experiments show that fine-tuning on speech synthesis assessment data consistently improves performance on both intelligibility and naturalness prediction, while joint training yields gains primarily on naturalness. These results suggest that synthesis artifacts and dysarthric speech share perceptual commonalities, and speech synthesis evaluation corpora offer a practical augmentation source that reduces reliance on scarce clinical annotations.

items.title: Clinically-Supervised Hierarchical LoRA-MoE: A Parameter-Efficient Framework for Severity-Aware Dysarthric Speech Assessment
items.authors: Jiaqi Wang(Xi'an Jiaotong University); Guanghua Xu(Xi'an Jiaotong University); Hongjie Zhou(Xi'an Jiaotong University); Shuwen Bai(Xi'an Jiaotong University); Sicong Zhang(Xi'an Jiaotong University)
items.abstract: Automatic dysarthria severity assessment is crucial for clinical monitoring yet hindered by data scarcity and pronounced speech heterogeneity. While self-supervised models such as WavLM provide strong representations, adapting them to low-resource medical domains remains challenging. We propose a Clinically-Supervised Hierarchical LoRA-MoE framework that freezes the WavLM backbone and introduces shared LoRA adapters in lower layers for general acoustic modeling, together with dynamically routed expert LoRAs in deeper layers for severity-specific patterns. A clinically-supervised router selectively activates expert parameters conditioned on utterance characteristics. Experiments on the UA-Speech corpus in 2- and 5-class settings demonstrate consistent improvements over full fine-tuning, achieving F1 scores of 94.54% and 61.55%, respectively.

items.title: A multilingual composite speech index to assess passage reading in Huntington’s disease
items.authors: Valentina G. Constantin(University College Dublin); Vitoria S. Fahed(University College Dublin); Emer P. Doheny(University College Dublin); Ruth Filan(University College Dublin); Carla Collazo(Universidad de Burgos); Joanna Krzysztofik(Institute of Psychiatry and Neurology); Elliot Mann(Cardiff University); Philippa Morgan-Jones(Cardiff University); Laura Mills(Cardiff University); Cheney Drew(Cardiff University); Anne E. Rosser(Cardiff University; Neuroscience and Mental Health Innovation Institute School of Medicine); Rebecca Cousins(North Bristol NHS Trust); Grzegorz Witkowski(Military Institute of Aviation Medicine); Esther Cubo(Hospital Universitario of Burgos); Monica Busse(King’s College London); Madeleine M. Lowery(University College Dublin)
items.abstract: Digital speech measures are a promising approach for assessing progression in Huntington's disease (HD). Reading tasks allow evaluation of both motor and cognitive dysfunction due to the high cognitive load involved. In this study, speech during passage reading was automatically detected and analyzed in 89 patients with HD and 82 matched controls in three languages (English, Polish, and Spanish). Bursts of voiced activity were identified through an adaptive thresholding method to estimate speech features. Significant differences in temporal features were observed between the HD and control groups. Features were then standardized to the language-matched controls and averaged to yield a composite temporal speech index (CTSI). Strong correlations were observed between CTSI and composite, cognitive, and motor scores from the Unified Huntington's Disease Rating Scale, with the highest correlation for the Symbol Digit Modality Test, which measures cognitive processing speed and attention.

items.title: Vowel Nasalization in Upper Airway Diseases: An Analysis Using the CUCO Database
items.authors: Yilan Wei(Independent Researcher); Qi Wang(Hunan University)
items.abstract: Upper airway diseases can affect speech by altering nasal airflow and nasal-oral resonance coupling. However, most existing studies rely on general acoustic features and lack systematic analyses of vowel nasalization directly related to nasal function. Using the CUCO database, this study analyzes vowel nasalization in patients undergoing septoplasty, endoscopic sinus surgery, or tonsillectomy, and in healthy controls, at pre- and postoperative time points. Two nasalization measures, A1-P0 and A1-P1, are examined across pathology type, temporal progression, and vowel category. Results show A1-P0 is more sensitive to pathology differences, and nasalization is vowel dependent, with /u/ most sensitive to resonance changes. Only the tonsillectomy group exhibits transient early postoperative nasalization changes; no long-term differences occur in other groups. These findings support the value of vowel nasalization measures for speech analysis in upper airway diseases.
