items.title: What Do Deepfake Speech Detectors Actually Hear?
items.authors: Vojtěch Staněk(Brno University of Technology); Veronika Jirmusová(Brno University of Technology); Anton Firc(Brno University of Technology); Kamil Malinka(Brno University of Technology); Jakub Reš(Brno University of Technology); Martin Perešíni(Brno University of Technology)
items.abstract: Deepfake speech detectors often output a single score without explaining why an audio sample is flagged, where in the signal the evidence lies, or what cues drive the decision. We propose an audio-native explainability pipeline using Integrated Gradients on time-aligned self-supervised representations to localize decision evidence over time. We apply the proposed method to three WavLM-based detectors (AASIST, CA-MHFA, SLS) on ASVspoof 5 and manually annotate the highest-attribution regions to provide a semantic meaning of the most important cues. Despite similar performance, the detectors rely on different cues: AASIST emphasizes non-speech/environment cues, CA-MHFA focuses on localized phoneme artifacts, and SLS relies on word boundaries and spectral integrity. We move beyond speculative reasoning and validate our findings by causal masking of the primary detector cues. Observed performance degradation further supports the explained detector semantics.

items.title: LISE : Listenable Interpretable Speaker Embeddings
items.authors: Xiaoliang Wu(University of Southampton); Chongxin Gan(Hong Kong PolyU); Ke Liu(University of Edinburgh); Peter Bell(University of Edinburgh); Jennifer Williams(University of Southampton)
items.abstract: Deep neural network-based automatic speaker verification (ASV) systems achieve impressive performance but their embedding representations remain opaque, lacking a structured and perceptually verifiable explanation of the vocal characteristics they encode. Existing approaches either require annotation of speaker attributes or introduce alternative representations whose interpretability is unvalidated with listeners. We propose Listenable Interpretable Speaker Embeddings (LISE), a label-free framework that decomposes pretrained speaker embeddings into a small set of components. This decomposition yields a structured representation that supports the analysis of what information has been encoded by speaker embeddings. LISE preserves ASV performance with negligible EER degradation on x-vector and ECAPA-TDNN. Crucially, the interpretability of these components for human listeners is demonstrated through listening experiments, where participants distinguished speakers with 83.9% accuracy.

items.title: Explainable and Trustworthy Speech Emotion Recognition Using Confidence Score and Reinforcement Learning Rectified Speech Emotion Descriptors
items.authors: Youjun Chen(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Xurong Xie(Chinese Academy of Sciences); Mengzhe Geng(National Research Council Canada); Zengrui Jin(Tsinghua University); Jiajun Deng(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Guinan Li(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Shujie Hu(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Huimeng Wang(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Haoning Xu(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Chengxi Deng(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Bowen Zhang(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Xunying Liu(The Chinese University of Hong Kong)
items.abstract: Explainable and trustworthy speech emotion recognition (SER) remains a challenging task to date, largely due to the scarcity of SER data with reliable speech emotion descriptor (SED) labels, such as prosodic features and speaker traits. This paper presents a confidence score and reinforcement learning (RL) based on-the-fly SED rectification approach for post-training SER systems on automatically annotated SED labels. Experiments on IEMOCAP and MELD suggest that explainable SER systems incorporating the proposed confidence score and RL-based SED rectification approach consistently outperform baselines without data selection or SED rectification. The best performing system, which integrates both components, surpasses the baseline without data selection and SED rectification, achieving SER gains of 2.9% and 3.3% absolute (3.7% and 5.4% relative) on IEMOCAP and MELD benchmarks, respectively.

items.title: FLiP: Towards understanding and interpreting multimodal multilingual sentence embeddings
items.authors: Santosh Kesiraju(Brno University of Technology); Bolaji Yusuf(Brno University of Technology); Šimon Sedláček(Brno University of Technology); Oldřich Plchot(Brno University of Technology); Petr Schwarz(Brno University of Technology)
items.abstract: This paper presents factorized linear projection (FLiP) models for understanding pretrained sentence embedding spaces. We train FLiP models to recover the lexical content from multilingual (LaBSE), multimodal (SONAR) and API-based (Gemini) sentence embedding spaces in several high- and mid-resource languages. We show that FLiP can recall more than 75% of lexical content from the embeddings, significantly outperforming existing non-factorized baselines. Using this as a diagnostic tool, we uncover the modality and language biases across the selected sentence encoders and provide practitioners with intrinsic insights about the encoders without relying on conventional downstream evaluation tasks. Our implementation is public.

items.title: Inside the Latent Flow: Causal Deciphering of Attention Dynamics in Audio Separation Foundation Models
items.authors: Yuxuan Chen(The Chinese University of Hong Kong; Jilin University); Haoyuan Yu(The Chinese University of Hong Kong; Hunan University); Peize He(University of Electronic Science and Technology of China)
items.abstract: Flow-matching transformers achieve strong audio separation, yet their attention dynamics are opaque. We adapt established causal-intervention principles into a deterministic, inference-time probing protocol for SAM Audio. Orthogonal probing uncovers a dual-pathway text-conditioning mechanism: additive injections control semantic identity, while cross-attention refines acoustic structure. We observe an asynchronous layerwise convergence: stable layers build temporal scaffolds early, whereas fast layers continue resolving artifacts during sampling. The model also attenuates temporal segmentation cues to maintain continuous-flow stability. Using these insights, we propose Layer-Selective Attention Caching (LSAC), a training-free acceleration method that caches attention in stable layers. Across acoustic complexities, LSAC cuts self-attention computation by ~25% with negligible quality loss and yields up to 6.7x higher quality retention than naive step reduction.

items.title: Towards Interpretable Framework for Neural Audio Codecs via Sparse Autoencoders: A Case Study on Accent Information
items.authors: Shih-Heng Wang(University of Southern California); Tiantian Feng(University of Southern California); Aditya Kommineni(University of Southern California); Thanathai Lertpetchpun(University of Southern California); Bowen Yi(University of Southern California); Xuan Shi(University of Southern California); Shrikanth Narayanan(University of Southern California)
items.abstract: Neural Audio Codecs (NACs) are widely adopted in modern speech systems, yet how they encode linguistic and paralinguistic information remains unclear. Improving the interpretability of NAC representations is critical for understanding and deploying them in sensitive applications. Hence, we employ Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to decompose dense NAC representations into sparse, interpretable activations. In this work, we focus on a challenging paralinguistic attribute-accent--and propose a framework to quantify NAC task-level interpretability. We evaluate four NAC models under 16 SAE configurations using a relative performance index. Our results show that DAC and SpeechTokenizer achieve the highest interpretability. We further reveal that acoustic-oriented NACs encode accent information primarily in activation magnitudes of sparse representations, whereas phonetic-oriented NACs rely more on activation positions, and that low-bitrate EnCodec variants show higher interpretability.

items.title: Spectro-Temporal Interference Confounds Phase Encoding in Spatial Audio Foundation Models
items.authors: Yuxuan Chen(The Chinese University of Hong Kong; Jilin University); Haoyuan Yu(The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen; Hunan University); Peize He(University of Electronic Science and Technology of China)
items.abstract: Recent spatial self supervised audio models achieve high performance on localization tasks, raising questions about their encoding of microsecond interaural phase fine structures. We propose a psychoacoustic benchmark based on the binaural masking level difference to evaluate this. Using an equalization cancellation baseline and a GCC PHAT positive control we evaluate nine frozen audio models spanning binaural SSL, monaural SSL, and neural audio codecs. Four monaural negative controls yield zero BMLD confirming binaural specificity. Two general purpose binaural SSL models exhibit minimal phase sensitivity while dedicated binaural spatial SSL models achieve substantial but sub-ceiling BMLD. Progressive physical ablations show that general purpose binaural SSL models rely on spectro temporal interference textures rather than cross channel phase computation. High detection rates in speech reflect a confounding reliance on broadband envelopes rather than genuine phase encoding.

items.title: On Optimizing Multimodal Jailbreaks for Spoken Language Models
items.authors: Aravind Krishnan(Saarland University; DFKI GmbH); Karolina Stańczak(ETH AI Center); Dietrich Klakow(Saarland University)
items.abstract: As Spoken Language Models (SLMs) integrate speech and text modalities, they inherit the safety vulnerabilities of their LLM backbone and an expanded attack surface. SLMs have previously been shown to be susceptible to jailbreaking, where adversarial prompts induce harmful responses. Yet existing attacks largely remain unimodal, optimizing either text or audio in isolation. We explore gradient-based multimodal jailbreaks and introduce JAMA (Joint Audio-text Multimodal Attack), a joint multimodal optimization framework combining Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG) and Projected Gradient Descent (PGD), simultaneously perturbing both input modalities. Evaluations across four state-of-the-art SLMs and four audio types demonstrate that JAMA surpasses unimodal jailbreak rate by 1.5× to 20×. We analyze the operational dynamics of this joint attack and show that a sequential attack makes it 4× to 6× faster. Our findings suggest that unimodal safety is insufficient for robust SLMs.

items.title: A Unified Safety Subspace Exists in Speech Language Models
items.authors: Nurdaulet Mukhituly(MBZUAI); Muhammad Cendekia Airlangga(MBZUAI); Rifo Ahmad Genadi(MBZUAI); Nhi Hoai Doan(MBZUAI); Amirbek Djanibekov(MBZUAI); Samuel Munachiso Nwadike(MBZUAI); Zangir Iklassov(MBZUAI); Kentaro Inui(MBZUAI; Tohoku University; RIKEN)
items.abstract: Speech Language Models (SLMs) extend large language models to spoken interaction, but this multimodal integration introduces modality-specific vulnerabilities. While prior work has typically addressed speech and text safety in isolation, our work uncovers a shared safety subspace where benign, harmful, and jailbreak representations exist regardless of input modality. We identify this subspace via a PCA projection, revealing a well-defined boundary separating refusal from jailbreak compliance. Causal intervention along this boundary shifts model behavior between refusal and compliance across modalities and attack types without additional training. For example, a refusal vector derived from an audio attack reduces text jailbreak success from 76.5% to 2.2%, while a refusal vector derived from the text attack reduces audio jailbreak success from 79.0% to 3.1%. We demonstrate these results on Qwen2-Audio and GLM-4-Voice, and confirm transferability across five different attacks.

items.title: Do Learned Layer Weights Reflect Pretrained Information Structure in Self-Supervised Speech Models?
items.authors: Yaroslav Getman(Aalto University, Finland); Tamás Grosz(Walton Institute, Ireland); Mikko Kurimo(Aalto University, Finland)
items.abstract: Self-supervised speech models are commonly evaluated using learned weighted sums over frozen layers. Prior work concluded these weights are uninformative, based on weak correlation with single-layer performance. In contrast, we explore whether learned weights reflect the pretrained model's layerwise information content, measured by adjusted mutual information (AMI) between clustered layer representations and phone or word labels. Across 13 SSL models, we find significant correlations for most conditions, with strength depending on supervision amount and pretraining objective. Weights after training with 10 minutes of labeled data consistently show higher correlation with AMI than those from 1 hour. Contrastive models show strong correlation of up to 0.98, while clustering-based ones yield weaker alignment. Despite prior characterizations as unreliable, learned weights systematically reflect pretrained information structure, particularly for contrastive models under limited supervision.

items.title: XAI-Grounded Explanation Generation for Speech Deepfake Detection with Training-Free Multimodal Large Language Models
items.authors: Yupei Li(Imperial College London; Technical University of Munich); Qiyang Sun(Imperial College London); Xiaoliang Wu(University of Southampton); Chenxi Wang(Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence); Berrak Sisman(Johns Hopkins University); Björn W. Schuller(Imperial College London; Technical University of Munich)
items.abstract: Speech deepfake detection (SDD) systems require trustworthy explanations for reliable decision-making. Existing explanation ways mainly fall into two categories. Traditional explainable AI (XAI), such as gradient-based attribution, produces low-level attribution signals tightly coupled with model decisions, and harder to be understood by human than natural language explanations. Meanwhile, large language model (LLM)-based explanation generation often produces generic and ungrounded descriptions due to the lack of heuristic evidence and task-specific supervision, stemming from limited grounded explanation datasets for SDD. We therefore propose a training-free explanation framework that integrates XAI evidence with multimodal LLMs to generate grounded and specific explanations. Using the PartialSpoof dataset, we construct a grounded explanation dataset and show that methods with XAI increase inside accuracy by over 45%, verified through human evaluation and faithfulness checks.

items.title: Cross-Attention is Half Explanation in Speech-to-Text Models
items.authors: Sara Papi(Fondazione Bruno Kessler); Dennis Fucci(Fondazione Bruno Kessler); Marco Gaido(Fondazione Bruno Kessler); Matteo Negri(Fondazione Bruno Kessler); Luisa Bentivogli(Fondazione Bruno Kessler)
items.abstract: Cross-attention is widely used in speech-to-text (S2T) systems and often exploited for downstream applications such as timestamp prediction and speech-text alignment, under the assumption that it reflects input-output dependencies. While extensively debated in NLP, its explanatory role remains underexplored in the speech domain. We empirically assess the explanatory power of cross-attention in S2T models by comparing attention scores with input saliency maps from feature-attribution methods. Our analysis spans monolingual and multilingual, single-task and multi-task models at multiple scales. We find moderate alignment between attention and saliency, particularly when aggregating across heads and layers. However, cross-attention captures only about 50% of input relevance and, at best, 52-75% of the encoder saliency. These results show that cross-attention offers useful but incomplete explanatory cues and should be interpreted with caution as a proxy for model behavior in S2T systems.

items.title: Causal Tracing of Audio-Text Fusion in Large Audio Language Models
items.authors: Wei-Chih Chen(National Taiwan University); Chien-yu Huang(Carnegie Mellon University); Hung-yi Lee(National Taiwan University; NTU Artificial Intelligence Center of Research Excellence)
items.abstract: Despite the strong performance of large audio language models (LALMs) in various tasks, exactly how and where they integrate acoustic features with textual context remains unclear. We adapt causal tracing to investigate the internal information flow of LALMs during audio comprehension. By conducting layer-wise and token-wise analyses across DeSTA, Qwen, and Voxtral, we evaluate the causal effects of individual hidden states. Layer-wise analysis identifies different fusion strategies, from progressive integration in DeSTA to an abrupt late-stage fusion in Qwen. Token-wise analysis shows that the final sequence token acts as an informational bottleneck where the network decisively retrieves relevant information from the audio. We also observe an attention-like query mechanism at intermediate token positions that triggers the model to pull task-relevant audio context. These findings provide a clear characterization of when and where multi-modal integration occurs within LALMs.

items.title: Disentangling Acoustic Cues in Alzheimer’s Pathology and Perception: The Roles of Language and Gender
items.authors: Liu He(University of Science and Technology of China); Yuanchao Li(University of Edinburgh); Yin-Long Liu(University of Science and Technology of China); Rui Feng(University of Science and Technology of China); Yiming Wang(University of Science and Technology of China); Jiaxin Chen(University of Science and Technology of China); Yizhe Wang(University of Science and Technology of China); Jiahong Yuan(University of Science and Technology of China)
items.abstract: Acoustic biomarkers show promise for detecting Alzheimer's Disease (AD), yet whether the cues driving diagnostic AI align with those salient to human listeners is underexplored across languages and genders, where pathological markers and perceptual strategies differ. We train models to predict clinical AD status (pathology) and human perceptual scores across Mandarin and Greek, male and female speakers. Using SHAP for interpretability and statistical models for validation, we compare feature importance by subgroup. Results reveal a context-dependent divergence: pathological–perceptual alignment is significant for Mandarin and female speakers but disappears for Greek and male speakers, where pathology models did not exceed chance—a failure mode population-specific auditing surfaces. Global Explainable AI (XAI) explanations can mask critical demographic divergences, highlighting the need for population-specific explainability auditing for equitable deployment of clinical speech AI.

items.title: Towards Dys-XAI: Influence-Based Explanations for Dysarthria Severity Assessment
items.authors: Xiaoliang Wu(University of Southampton); Qiyang Sun(Imperial College London); Yupei Li(Imperial College London); Erfan Loweimi(University of Edinburgh); Jennifer Williams(University of Southampton); Zhengjun Yue(King's College London)
items.abstract: Dysarthria severity assessment is essential for therapy planning and longitudinal monitoring, yet manual perceptual rating is time-consuming and variable across clinicians. Although deep learning models achieve strong performance, their black-box nature limits clinical adoption. Existing speech explainability methods typically provide acoustic feature importance scores that are difficult for end-users to interpret. We propose an influence-based, instance-level explainability framework that explains each decision through supportive and competing training samples. Using gradient-based influence approximations, we compute per-utterance influence scores to identify supportive and competing training samples for each prediction. Controlled deletion experiments (5-20%) validate the explanations, showing that removing highly influential samples systematically shifts predictions. This approach provides auditable explanations by linking decisions to perceptible reference cases.

items.title: What Do Neural Networks Learn for TDOA Estimation? A Cross-Architecture Probing Study
items.authors: Yaozhong Kang(Institute of Science Tokyo); Jiang Wang(Institute of Science Tokyo); Runwu Shi(Institute of Science Tokyo); Takeshi Ashizawa(Institute of Science Tokyo); Benjamin Yen(Institute of Science Tokyo); Kazuhiro Nakadai(Institute of Science Tokyo)
items.abstract: Neural networks outperform classical GCC-PHAT for Time-Difference-of-Arrival (TDOA) estimation in noise and reverberation, yet their internal strategy remains unexplored. To uncover it, we turn GCC-PHAT's mathematical steps into diagnostic targets, probing hidden layers of three architectures (MLP, CNN, Transformer) and complementing with gradient attribution and causal frequency masking. We find that cross-power computation consistently emerges across all architectures and conditions, while PHAT whitening, the defining step of GCC-PHAT, fails to emerge. Instead, networks learn a magnitude-aware frequency weighting that preserves per-frequency reliability information discarded by PHAT. This makes PHAT an information bottleneck: removing it from both classical and neural GCC pipelines improves performance under additive noise. On real-world reverberant data, PHAT remains the best classical weighting, but end-to-end networks achieve lower error by learning data-adaptive weighting.

items.title: TSExplorer: An interactive data annotation and exploration tool for time-series data
items.authors: Einari Vaaras(Tampere University); Manu Airaksinen(University of Helsinki); Okko Räsänen(Tampere University)
items.abstract: We present TSExplorer, a cross-platform tool for interactive annotation and exploration of time-series data. The tool enables users to inspect high-dimensional datasets through multiple complementary 2D visualizations derived from high-dimensional feature representations. TSExplorer is designed as a general-purpose research tool supporting a wide range of workflows, including exploratory data analysis, annotation of unlabeled or partially-labeled datasets, comparison of feature representations, and post-hoc inspection and refinement of existing labels with interactive visual feedback.

items.title: Lightweight Emotion Recognition with Disjoint Modality Fusion
items.authors: Serkan Sulun(INESC TEC; University of Porto)
items.abstract: Modern speech emotion recognition methods typically use large-scale models and multimodal fusion, often resulting in significant computational overhead that limits real-world deployment on consumer hardware. We propose Light-DMF, a lightweight model designed to classify emotions from audio and text both independently and through a fused pathway. Our disjoint architecture supports mixed-modal data where audio or text can be present, absent, or contain conflicting emotional cues and labels. Our model has fewer than 65k trainable parameters and achieves a real-time factor below 1 in CPU-only inference. We provide open-source code and a demo to facilitate future research and offer a speech emotion recognition tool for the general public.

items.title: SpeechBench: A Unified Speech Annotation and Analysis Tool
items.authors: Zheng Nan(University of New South Wales); Tharmakulasingam Sirojan(University of New South Wales); Mostafa Shahin(University of New South Wales); Tünde Szalay(University of Sydney); Vidhyasaharan Sethu(University of New South Wales); Beena Ahmed(University of New South Wales)
items.abstract: Existing speech annotation tools do not adequately support model-assisted manual annotation workflows that use general-purpose models to pre-annotate domain-specific speech data followed by human refinement. As a result, the annotation process remains time-consuming, inefficient, and difficult to scale. We therefore present SpeechBench, an integrated tool designed to facilitate this workflow. The tool incorporates trained models for a range of speech processing tasks and provides a graphical interface for constructing multi-step, model-based pre-annotation pipelines, lowering the barrier for non-technical users. It also supports flexible deployment on private servers to meet strict data privacy requirements.

items.title: corpusgen: An Open-Source Toolkit for Phoneme-Coverage-Optimized Speech Corpus Design Across Languages
items.authors: Muntaser Syed(Florida Institute of Technology); Marius Silaghi(Florida Institute of Technology); Sharun Akter Khushbu(Daffodil International University); Fariha Jaigirdar(Deakin University)
items.abstract: We present corpusgen, an open-source Python toolkit for designing speech corpora with maximal phoneme coverage across languages. The toolkit integrates grapheme-to-phoneme conversion via espeak-ng, phoneme inventories from PHOIBLE (covering 2,186 languages), and multiple corpus optimization algorithms including greedy set cover with CELF acceleration, integer linear programming, distribution-aware selection, and NSGA-II multi-objective optimization. Beyond selection from existing text, corpusgen supports targeted sentence generation through pluggable backends including LLM APIs and local transformer models with phonotactic control. A unified evaluation module reports phoneme, diphone, and triphone coverage alongside distribution quality metrics. The toolkit is pip-installable, provides both a Python API and a CLI, and is released under the Apache-2.0 license. We demonstrate its application to corpus design across typologically diverse languages, showing how coverage-optimized selection achieves near-optimal phoneme coverage with significantly fewer sentences than random baselines.

items.title: Speech Playground: An Interactive Tool for Speech Analysis and Comparison
items.authors: Stephen McIntosh(The University of Tokyo); Daisuke Saito(The University of Tokyo); Nobuaki Minematsu(The University of Tokyo)
items.abstract: This paper presents Speech Playground, an interactive speech visualization and comparison tool. While existing tools such as Praat are excellent, it can be cumbersome to integrate them with modern deep learning representations and use them for comparison. Speech Playground addresses this by combining a Python backend with a web-based frontend for interactive exploration of multiple feature types, including continuous, discrete, and variable-length representations. It includes TextGrid and forced alignment support together with configurable distance and alignment settings for visual and auditory comparison. Speech Playground is intended for use in speech research, representation validation, and computer-aided pronunciation training (CAPT)-oriented experimentation.

items.title: MER-Live: An Interactive Browser Demo of Prosody-Driven Multimodal Emotion Recognition
items.authors: Haoyu Song(Singapore Institute of Technology); Xiaoxiao Miao(Duke Kunshan University); Pai Chet Ng(Singapore Institute of Technology); Timothy Liu(NVIDIA AI Technology Center); Aik Beng Ng(NVIDIA AI Technology Center); Ian McLoughlin(Singapore Institute of Technology)
items.abstract: MER-Live is a real-time multimodal emotion recognition demo in which speech is the dominant signal, supported by video and lexical cues. The acoustic branch uses a novel lightweight masked auto-encoder SER model (MSMC) on log-mel spectrograms, while the text branch acts only as an auxiliary tie-breaker rather than a keyword trigger. Users speak to the camera and watch emotion estimates update four times per second. They can hot-swap ten speaker-holdout checkpoints, record a five second utterance for IEMOCAP-style logit averaging, or upload audio files for side-by-side comparison with an open SER baseline. The 6.77M-parameter audio model, exported to TensorRT FP16, serves a batch of five in 0.24 ms on one H200, giving a 14x speed-up over PyTorch FP32. On 10-fold IEMOCAP, the deployed audio-only MSMC checkpoint used in MER-Live reaches 74.03% WA and 66.39% UA. Multimodal performance exceeds 83%.

items.title: Bio-Informed Speech Processing, Modeling, and Generation
items.abstract: Survey talk opening the Modeling Articulation oral session. The official program grid preserves the title but not a full abstract in the exported sheet. Treat it as a survey of biologically informed approaches to speech processing, articulatory modeling, and generation, and do not invent specific claims, datasets, or results.

items.title: ArtBoost: Synthetic Articulatory Data Augmentation for Acoustic-to-Articulatory Inversion
items.authors: Hyung Kyu Kim(Chung-Ang University); Byungchan Hwang(Chung-Ang University); Hak Gu Kim(Chung-Ang University)
items.abstract: Recent acoustic-to-articulatory inversion (AAI) models rely on electromagnetic articulography (EMA) data, which are costly and limited in scale. To address this limitation, we propose ArtBoost, a novel data augmentation strategy that leverages large-scale speech-mesh datasets originally developed for speech-driven 3D facial animation to improve AAI under limited EMA supervision. ArtBoost extracts pseudo articulatory trajectories from visible facial anchors and uses them for pre-training before fine-tuning on real EMA data. Experiments show consistent improvements in PCC and RMSE. Trajectory analyses confirm that the pseudo articulatory signals reflect physically meaningful visible articulatory dynamics. Additional evaluations across different AAI architectures demonstrate stable performance gains, indicating that ArtBoost can be integrated into diverse AAI models. These results suggest that speech-mesh data provide an effective and scalable source of articulatory supervision for AAI. Project page: https://cau-irislab. github.io/Interspeech26-ArtBoost/

items.title: STArK: Towards Synthesizing Articulatory Kinematics from Text
items.authors: Xavier Yin(Carnegie Mellon University); Carlos Busso(Carnegie Mellon University)
items.abstract: Recent deep learning approaches in modeling articulatory kinematics have shown success in mapping speech audio to electromagnetic articulography (EMA) kinematics, but these methods are limited by the scarcity of high-quality articulatory datasets. We introduce synthesizing text to articulatory kinematics (STArK), which offers a novel approach in generating articulatory kinematics directly from text. We train STArK on the LibriTTS-R dataset with pseudo-labeled EMA features derived from a pre-trained speech-to-articulation model. STArK is the first model to demonstrate high-quality articulatory kinematics generation from text. STArK achieves comparable performance to existing multi-speaker text-to-speech models at speech synthesis, while supporting voice cloning without seeing speaker embeddings during training. STArK aims to enable the generation of scalable articulatory data from text corpora for downstream tasks.

items.title: Physics-Informed Neural Operator for Speech Production Analysis
items.authors: Kazuya Yokota(Nagaoka University of Technology); Xinmeng Luan(McGill University); Debasish Ray Mohapatra(University of British Columbia); Gary Scavone(McGill University); Sidney Fels(University of British Columbia)
items.abstract: Physics-informed neural operators (PINOs) have recently gained attention as fast numerical simulators with potential for solving inverse problems. This study proposes the first PINO-based method for speech production analysis. The model learns the governing one-dimensional wave equations directly without requiring pre-computed supervised training data. Using vocal tract shape data as input features, we compare the proposed model's predicted f0, glottal volume velocity and sound pressure at the lip for five static vowels to a conventional Runge Kutta/Finite difference approach. With errors of 0.8% for glottal volume flow and 3.2% for speech waveforms, the proposed model enables efficient GPU-parallelized simulation without iterative calculations. We conclude that PINO is a promising approach for fast analysis of speech.

items.title: PyPhonPlan: Simulating phonetic planning with dynamic neural fields and task dynamics
items.authors: Sam Kirkham(Lancaster University)
items.abstract: We introduce PyPhonPlan, a Python toolkit for implementing dynamical models of phonetic planning using coupled dynamic neural fields and task dynamic simulations. The toolkit provides modular components for defining planning, perception and memory fields, as well as between-field coupling, gestural inputs, and using field activation profiles to solve tract variable trajectories. We illustrate the toolkit's capabilities through an example application: simulating production/perception loops with a coupled memory field, which demonstrates the framework's ability to model interactive speech dynamics using representations that are temporally-principled, neurally-grounded, and phonetically-rich. PyPhonPlan is released as open-source software and contains executable examples to promote reproducibility, extensibility, and cumulative computational development for speech communication research.

title: Speaker Privacy and Anonymization
header: Thursday 1 October 2026 - 09:00-11:00 - Area 4 - Oral 6 - Speaker Privacy and Anonymization

items.title: Privacy vs. Performance: Assessing Communication Utility of Anonymized Voice Features
items.authors: Amanda Chan(Educational Testing Service); Chee Wee Leong(Educational Testing Service); Candy Olivia Mawalim(Japan Advanced Institute of Science and Technology); Shogo Okada(Japan Advanced Institute of Science and Technology)
items.abstract: Voice anonymization is essential for protecting user privacy, yet it may distort acoustic cues that are critical for communication assessment. In this work, we study the impact of phase vocoder time-scale modification (PV-TSM), a lightweight anonymization technique selected for operational efficiency, on acoustic and prosodic feature preservation. We integrate PV-TSM into an end-to-end speech analysis pipeline and evaluate its effects on acoustic features as well as automatic speech recognition (ASR) performance. Our results show that anonymization can largely preserve these features while effectively masking speaker identity. Further, fine-tuning the ASR model with anonymized speech mitigates recognition errors and restores downstream feature accuracy. These findings demonstrate that privacy protection and prosodic fidelity can coexist, enabling reliable communication assessment in privacy-sensitive contexts.

items.title: DiffAnon: Diffusion-based Prosody Control for Voice Anonymization
items.authors: Ismail Rasim Ulgen(Johns Hopkins University); Zexin Cai(Johns Hopkins University); Nicholas Andrews(Johns Hopkins University); Philipp Koehn(Johns Hopkins University); Berrak Sisman(Johns Hopkins University)
items.abstract: To preserve or not to preserve prosody is a central question in voice anonymization. Prosody conveys meaning and affect, yet is tightly coupled with speaker identity. Existing methods either discard prosody for privacy or lack a principled mechanism to control the utility-privacy trade-off, operating at fixed design points. We propose DiffAnon, a diffusion-based anonymization method with classifier-free guidance (CFG) that provides explicit, continuous inference-time control over prosody preservation. DiffAnon refines acoustic detail over semantic embeddings of an RVQ codec, enabling smooth interpolation between anonymization strength and prosodic fidelity within a single model. To the best of our knowledge, it is the first voice anonymization framework to provide structured, interpolatable inference-time prosody control. Experiments demonstrate structured trade-off behavior, achieving strong utility while maintaining competitive privacy across controllable operating points.

items.title: DP-VOXLET: Provable Speaker Anonymization for Disentangled Speech Representations
items.authors: Ivoline Ngong(University of Vermont); Jack D'Iorio(University of Vermont); Hailey Schoppe(University of Vermont); Christopher Liberatore(Galois, Inc.); Nichole Schimanski(Galois, Inc.); Taisa Kushner(Galois, Inc.); Joseph P. Near(University of Vermont)
items.abstract: Systems for speaker anonymization obfuscate the speaker of an utterance, while maintaining its original semantic contents and prosody. Recent solutions for speaker anonymization rely on learned representations that disentangle an utterance into semantic contents and speaker properties. To anonymize an utterance, these systems replace the speaker properties while leaving the semantic contents unchanged—an approach that can produce strong results on empirical measures of privacy. In this work, we introduce speaker differential privacy, a formal definition of speaker anonymization based on the framework of differential privacy, and a mechanism for speaker anonymization that provably satisfies the definition. In contrast to prior heuristic-based anonymization systems, our approach enables a provable lower bound on re-identification success rate (e.g. equal error rate) for any possible adversary. We implement our approach in a framework that is compatible with existing disentangled representations. Compared to the prior work on differential privacy for speaker anonymization, our approach achieves significantly higher utility.

items.title: Voice Privacy from an Attribute-based Perspective
items.authors: Mehtab Ur Rahman(Centre for Language Studies); Martha Larson(Centre for Language Studies; Radboud University); Cristian Tejedor-Garcia(Centre for Language Studies)
items.abstract: Voice privacy approaches that preserve the anonymity of speakers modify speech in an attempt to break the link with the true identity of the speaker. Current benchmarks measure speaker protection based on signal-to-signal comparisons. In this paper, we introduce an attribute-based perspective, where we measure privacy protection in terms of comparisons between sets of speaker attributes. First, we analyze privacy impact by calculating speaker uniqueness for ground truth attributes, attributes inferred on the original speech, and attributes inferred on speech protected with standard anonymization. Next, we examine a threat scenario involving only a single utterance per speaker and calculate attack error rates. Overall, we observe that inferred attributes still present a risk despite attribute inference errors. Our research points to the importance of considering both attribute-related threats and protection mechanisms in future voice privacy research.

items.title: Acoustic token admixture for joint speaker and content anonymization
items.authors: Ali Golmakani(Nijta SAS); Seyed Ahmad Hosseini(Nijta SAS); Omar Manil Bendali(Nijta SAS); Emmanuel Vincent(Nijta SAS; Université de Lorraine); Brij Mohan Lal Srivastava(Nijta SAS)
items.abstract: Speech recordings in regulated domains cannot be shared or reused for AI development without suppressing two independent re-identification channels: biometric speaker identity and linguistically identifying content. Existing approaches address each channel in isolation and require full re-synthesis, sacrificing the in-domain acoustic characteristics that make recordings valuable. We propose a unified acoustic token-space framework that jointly anonymizes both channels via per-frame admixture of encoder-derived and phoneme-conditioned tokens, with NER-triggered span replacement preserving surrounding prosody. On the VoicePrivacy 2024 benchmark the system achieves EER 42.54%, within one point of the challenge top submission, with WER 3.73%.

items.title: Privacy-Preserving End-to-End Full-Duplex Speech Dialogue Models
items.authors: Nikita Kuzmin(NTU; A*STAR); Tao Zhong(Huawei; CUHK); Jiajun Deng(Huawei); Yingke Zhu(Huawei); Tristan Tsoi(Huawei); Tianxiang Cao(Huawei); Simon Lui(Huawei); Kong Aik Lee(Hong Kong PolyU); Eng Siong Chng(NTU)
items.abstract: End-to-end full-duplex speech models feed user audio through an always-on LLM backbone, yet the speaker privacy implications of their hidden representations remain unexamined. Following the VoicePrivacy 2024 protocol with a lazy-informed attacker, we show that the hidden states of SALM-Duplex and Moshi leak substantial speaker identity across probed transformer layers. Layer-wise and turn-wise analyses reveal that leakage persists across these layers, with SALM-Duplex showing stronger leakage in early layers while Moshi leaks uniformly, and that Linkability rises sharply in the first few turns. We propose two streaming anonymization setups using Stream-Voice-Anon: a waveform-level front-end (Anon-W2W) and a feature-domain replacement (Anon-W2F). Anon-W2F raises EER over 3.5× relative to the discrete encoder baseline (11.2%→41.0%), approaching the 50% chance ceiling, while Anon-W2W retains 78-93% of baseline sBERT across setups with sub-second first response latency (FRL under 0.8 s).

title: Speech signal analysis
header: Thursday 1 October 2026 - 09:00-11:00 - Area 5 - Oral 7 - Speech signal analysis

items.title: Factorization and Latent Structure in Speech Representations
items.abstract: Structure in speech representations facilitates controlled generation, transfer to new domains, and analysis of model behavior. This talk surveys methods for imposing and discovering structure in speech representations. We give an overview of top-down techniques for imposing structure on learned representations, including the use of factorized training objectives, model distillation, and explicit bottlenecks or interpretable control variables. We discuss the advantages and limitations of this approach and contrast them with bottom-up techniques, including probing, controlled perturbations, latent-space arithmetic, and resynthesis, for discovering and exploiting pre-existing structure in large pre-trained models. We conclude by discussing applications enabled by such structure, including controllable generation and editing, voice conversion, domain transfer, efficient speech modeling, and the separation or attribution of multiple speakers.

items.title: Multilingual Word-Level Forced Alignment with Self-Supervised Representations and Learned Dynamic Programming
items.authors: Roy Weber(Technion – Israel Institute of Technology); Meidan Zehavi(Technion – Israel Institute of Technology); Rotem Rousso(Technion – Israel Institute of Technology); Joseph Keshet(Technion – Israel Institute of Technology)
items.abstract: We present a method for accurate multilingual word-level forced alignment, consisting of an alignment encoder and a learned alignment decoder. The encoder integrates two representations: one from the Massively Multilingual Speech (MMS) model and another from a self-supervised phoneme boundary detector (UnSupSeg). It learns to fuse them and to estimate word-boundary probabilities over long temporal contexts. The alignment decoder is a learned dynamic programming that combines encoder outputs with segmental features over the MMS and UnSupSeg representations to infer final word boundaries. Trained iteratively on TIMIT and Buckeye, the proposed approach outperforms Montreal Forced Aligner (MFA) and MMS-based alignment on both datasets. On unseen languages (Dutch, German, and Hebrew), the proposed model achieves performance consistently better than or on par with existing alignment approaches, indicating its potential to scale to 1100+ languages supported by MMS without further training.

items.title: V-Align: Visual Forced Alignment via Phoneme to Video Optimal Path Traversal
items.authors: Souvik Ghosh(IIIT Hyderabad); C. V. Jawahar(IIIT Hyderabad); Vinay Namboodiri(University of Bath)
items.abstract: Visual Forced Alignment (VFA) aims to temporally localize linguistic units within silent talking-face videos, enabling alignment when audio is noisy or unavailable. We propose V-Align, a structured framework that formulates VFA as an optimal monotonic path traversal problem over a frame-phoneme compatibility lattice. Given the lip-motion embeddings and transcript-derived phoneme representations, V-Align learns a soft traversal posterior and recovers discrete boundaries via dynamic programming. Training follows a two-stage strategy: Stage 1 encourages optimal path learning without explicit boundary supervision and already achieves competitive performance relative to fully supervised VFA baselines, while Stage 2 refines boundary precision using additional word-level supervision. Experiments on LRS2 and LRS3 demonstrate state-of-the-art MAE and frame accuracy. Code and demo are available at: https://valign-interspeech.github.io/.

items.title: findsylls: A Language‑Agnostic Toolkit for Syllable‑Level Speech Tokenization and Embedding
items.authors: Héctor Javier Vázquez Martínez(University of Pennsylvania)
items.abstract: Syllable-level units offer compact and linguistically meaningful representations for spoken language modeling and unsupervised word discovery, but research on syllabification remains fragmented across disparate implementations, datasets, and evaluation protocols. We introduce findsylls, a modular, language-agnostic toolkit that unifies classical syllable detectors and end-to-end syllabifiers under a common interface for syllable segmentation, embedding extraction, and multi-granular evaluation. The toolkit implements and standardizes widely used methods (e.g., Sylber, VG-HuBERT) and allows their components to be recombined, enabling controlled comparisons of representations, algorithms, and token rates. We demonstrate findsylls on English and Spanish corpora and on new hand-annotated data from Kono, an underdocumented Central Mande language, illustrating how a single framework can support reproducible syllable-level experiments across both high-resource and under-resourced settings.

items.title: Duration-Aware Soft Targets for Text-Independent Supervised Phone Segmentation
items.authors: Raghavan Ramesh(IIT Hyderabad); Meka Nani(IIT Hyderabad); Sri Rama Murty Kodukula(IIT Hyderabad)
items.abstract: Hard boundaries are commonly used as ground truth targets for text-independent supervised phone segmentation. However, prior works do not explicitly model the uncertainty in phone transition annotations. To address this limitation, we propose the use of soft targets in place of hard boundaries. The ambiguity of transition around boundary events is modeled using two unnormalized zero-mean half Gaussian pulses centered at each boundary indicated by the hard targets, with standard deviations proportional to neighboring segment durations. Hard labels within two standard deviations of the boundary are replaced with Gaussian function values, while the other labels remain unchanged. Using soft targets, a baseline BiGRU model achieves an R-val of 91.53% on the TIMIT test split. Experiments on out-of-domain and multilingual data show statistically significant improvements over hard targets.

title: LLM Based Speech Synthesis
header: Thursday 1 October 2026 - 09:00-11:00 - Area 7 - Oral 7 - LLM Based Speech Synthesis

items.title: Decoding Order Matters in Autoregressive Speech Synthesis
items.authors: Minghui Zhao(University of Sheffield); Anton Ragni(University of Sheffield)
items.abstract: Autoregressive speech synthesis has traditionally followed a left-to-right order, yet generation order is a modelling choice. This paper investigates decoding order through a masked diffusion framework that enables arbitrary decoding orders at inference time. To isolate the effect of decoding order from inductive biases introduced by learned discrete encoders, we operate on scalar quantised Mel-spectrograms. Our results demonstrate that the left-to-right strategy is suboptimal for capturing complex acoustic dependencies. The reverse, right-to-left, order consistently outperforms the traditional approach, while the adaptive confidence-based strategy top1 achieves the highest Mean Opinion Score (MOS) among all model outputs. Analysis reveals that the most effective orders maintain local clusters of consecutive frames to balance long-range temporal dependencies with local coherence. These results establish decoding order as a critical parameter for improving synthesis quality.

items.title: Decoupling Search and Evaluation: Efficient Beam Decoding for Language Model-Based Text-to-Speech Synthesis
items.authors: Chenlin Liu(Harbin Institute of Technology); Jie Gao(Tsinghua University); Wei Zhou(Zhejiang University); Guangyan Zhang(Zhejiang University); Minghui Fang(Tsinghua University); Jiqing Han(Harbin Institute of Technology)
items.abstract: Language model (LM)-based text-to-speech (TTS) systems typically rely on sampling-based decoding, which suffers from stochastic instability. While beam search offers a maximization-based alternative, it is limited in speech generation due to severe degeneration (e.g., temporal collapse) and high latency. Our analysis reveals that beam search cost is highly imbalanced between search and evaluation stages. Motivated by this, we propose Search-and-eValuatE beam decoding (SaVE-Beam), which decouples hypothesis expansion from sequence scoring. Specifically, a lightweight student model performs chunk-wise beam construction, while the teacher LM retains exact evaluation. Hard repetition constraints are introduced to prevent degenerate loops. Experiments show that SaVE-Beam achieves up to 5.1x speedup over conventional beam search without degrading speech quality, and reduces WER by up to 50% compared to sampling, enabling practical maximization-based decoding for real-time LM-based TTS.

items.title: Eliminating Stability Hallucinations in LLM-based TTS models via Attention Guidance
items.authors: Shiming Wang(University of Science and Technology of China); Zhihao Du(Independent Researcher); Yang Xiang(Independent Researcher); Tianyu Zhao(Independent Researcher); Han Zhao(Independent Researcher); Qian Chen(Independent Researcher); Xiangang Li(Independent Researcher); Hanjie Guo(University of Science and Technology of China); ZhenHua Ling(University of Science and Technology of China)
items.abstract: This paper focuses on resolving stability hallucinations (e.g., repetitive or omitted speech) in LLM-based Text-to-Speech (TTS) models by improving and leveraging the attention mechanism. First, we analyzed the alignment mechanism between text tokens and speech tokens in LLMs. We then proposed a metric termed the Optimal Alignment Score (OAS), which employs the Viterbi algorithm to evaluate text-speech alignment quality. Subsequently, OAS was integrated into the training of CosyVoice2 to assist LLMs in learning continuous, stable alignment. Additionally, the pre-trained attention value is employed to guide the training of the student CosyVoice2 via chain-of-thought (CoT), which further reduces stability hallucinations in synthesized speech. Experiments on the Seed-TTS-Eval and CV3-Eval test sets demonstrate that the proposed methods can effectively reduce the stability hallucinations of CosyVoice2 without introducing additional negative effects. The appendix is available at https://wsmzzz.github.io/llm_attn/ index.html.

items.title: MamTra: A Hybrid Mamba-Transformer Backbone for Speech Synthesis
items.authors: Tan Dat Nguyen(Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology); Sangmin Bae(Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology); Joon Son Chung(Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology); Ji-Hoon Kim(Chung-Ang University)
items.abstract: Despite the remarkable quality of LLM-based text-to-speech systems, their reliance on autoregressive Transformers leads to quadratic computational complexity, which severely limits practical applications. Linear-time alternatives, notably Mamba, offer a potential remedy; however, they often sacrifice the global context essential for expressive synthesis. In this paper, we propose MamTra, an interleaved Mamba-Transformer framework designed to leverage the advantages of Mamba's efficiency and Transformers' modeling capability. We also introduce novel knowledge transfer strategies to distill insights from a pretrained Transformer into our hybrid architecture, thereby bypassing the prohibitive costs of training from scratch. Systematic experiments identify the optimal hybrid configuration, and demonstrate that MamTra reduces inference VRAM usage by up to 34% without compromising speech fidelity-even trained on only 2% of the original training dataset. Audio samples are available at.

items.title: DLLM-TTS: Block Discrete Diffusion Language Model for Text-to-Speech Synthesis
items.authors: Wasim Madha(Smallest.ai); Nityanand Mathur(Smallest.ai); Hamees Sayed(Smallest.ai); Apoorv Singh(Smallest.ai); Sameer Khurana(Smallest.ai); Akshat Mandloi(Smallest.ai); Sudarshan Kamath(Smallest.ai)
items.abstract: Current text-to-speech systems face a trade-off: autoregressive codec language models produce highly intelligible speech but require large-scale models and training data and decode tokens sequentially, while non-autoregressive approaches improve speed at the cost of linguistic accuracy. We present DLLM-TTS, a framework that formulates TTS as conditional block discrete diffusion over X-Codec2 neural audio codec tokens. The model decomposes sequences into blocks and applies masked diffusion within each block while processing blocks sequentially, learning both local acoustic coherence and global text-speech alignment. During inference, parallel token prediction within blocks enables efficient generation with a real-time factor (RTF) of 0.15. A 0.6B-parameter model trained on 20K hours achieves competitive performance on the Seed-TTS-eval benchmark, demonstrating that block discrete diffusion language models enable practical and data-efficient speech synthesis with parallel generation.

items.title: Bagpiper-TTS: Natural Language Guided Universal Speech Synthesis
items.authors: Jinchuan Tian(Carnegie Mellon University); Haoran Wang(Carnegie Mellon University); Siddhant Arora(Carnegie Mellon University); Takashi Maekaku(LY Corporation); Keita Goto(LY Corporation); Jin Sakuma(LY Corporation); Yusuke Shinohara(LY Corporation); Chao-Han Huck Yang(NVIDIA Research); Shinji Watanabe(Carnegie Mellon University)
items.abstract: Classical TTS systems typically rely on rigid input formats and predefined metadata slots, limiting their ability to fulfill flexible user requirements. This paper introduces Bagpiper-TTS, a universal speech synthesis system that deals with diverse natural language user requests. Given a natural language prompt, Bagpiper-TTS first reasons over the user’s intent to derive a rich caption, i.e., a comprehensive textual blueprint encompassing both transcription and nuanced metadata. Subsequently, this caption guides the synthesis of the target speech. Our model inherently supports a broad spectrum of tasks besides classical TTS applications, including multi-talker, intent-to-speech, roleplay synthesis, singing voice synthesis, and more. Experimental results demonstrate that Bagpiper-TTS achieves an 1.7% Word Error Rate (WER) on the Seed-TTS-Eval benchmark and match the performance of dedicated models in both LLM-as-a-judge and human subjective evaluations across multiple application.

title: New Training Methods for ASR
header: Thursday 1 October 2026 - 09:00-11:00 - Area 8 - Oral 2 - New Training Methods for ASR

items.title: Reducing the Offline-Streaming Gap for Unified ASR Transducer with Consistency Regularization
items.authors: Andrei Andrusenko(NVIDIA, Armenia); Vladimir Bataev(NVIDIA, Armenia); Lilit Grigoryan(NVIDIA, Armenia); Nune Tadevosyan(NVIDIA, Armenia); Vitaly Lavrukhin(NVIDIA, USA); Boris Ginsburg(NVIDIA, USA)
items.abstract: Unification of automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems reduces development and maintenance costs, but training a single model to perform well in both offline and low-latency streaming settings remains challenging. We present a Unified ASR framework for Transducer (RNNT) training that supports both offline and streaming decoding within a single model, using chunk-limited attention with right context and dynamic chunked convolutions. To further close the gap between offline and streaming performance, we introduce an efficient Triton implementation of mode-consistency regularization for RNNT (MCR-RNNT), which encourages agreement across training modes. Experiments show that the proposed approach improves streaming accuracy at low latency while preserving offline performance and scaling to larger model sizes and training datasets. The proposed Unified ASR framework and the English model checkpoint are open-sourced.

items.title: BACON: Boundary-Aware Convolution for Streaming Conformer Models
items.authors: Hainan Xu(NVIDIA corporation.); Kunal Dhawan(NVIDIA corporation.); Dongji Gao(NVIDIA corporation.); Jagadeesh Balam(NVIDIA corporation.)
items.abstract: We propose Boundary-Aware CONvolution (BACON), a drop-in replacement for causal convolution in streaming sequence tasks that leverage chunk-based Conformers. Streaming Conformers typically pair chunked attention with causal convolution to prevent future information leakage. We show that causal convolution is unnecessarily restrictive: within a chunk, all frames are already available, so the convolution kernel can safely look ahead up to the chunk boundary without violating the streaming constraint. BACON exploits this by splitting the depthwise convolution channels into a causal group and a boundary-aware bidirectional group, yielding a wider effective receptive field than the causal baseline while preserving parameter count. Across single-speaker Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), multi-speaker ASR, and speech-to-text translation tasks with two model architectures, BACON improves model accuracy while maintaining comparable latency.

items.title: Progressive Alignment Objectives for Aligner-Encoder based ASR
items.authors: Jaeyoung Lee(NTT, Inc.); Masato Mimura(NTT, Inc.); Takafumi Moriya(NTT, Inc.)
items.abstract: Aligner-Encoders are recently proposed seq2seq end-to-end ASR models that replace decoder attention by predicting the u-th token directly from the u-th encoder position, so the encoder must learn the alignment internally without cross-attention or a transducer lattice. In practice, this alignment often forms abruptly in the upper layers, making training sensitive and brittle on long utterances. We propose InterAligner, which adds an intermediate Aligner objective so alignment can form progressively across depth, together with an intermediate CTC loss (InterCTC) to stabilize optimization. On LibriSpeech with a 17-layer Conformer, a final-only Aligner reaches 5.0/7.8 WER (test-clean/other). InterCTC improves to 3.4/6.0, and InterAligner further reduces WER to 3.1/5.6 with the largest gains on long utterances.

items.title: From Bilevel to Trilevel: Joint Training for Speech Recognition
items.authors: Jen-Tzung Chien(National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University); Yu-Chun Lin(National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University); Xiaodong Cui(IBM T. J. Watson Research Center)
items.abstract: This paper presents the practical optimization strategies to extend the bilevel learning into a trilevel setting for speech recognition. This method jointly trains an acoustic model according to supervised, unsupervised, and distilled learning objectives. To make trilevel training feasible in large-scale ASR models, we employ a sequential penalty-based bilevel gradient descent method that collapses the lower two levels into a bilevel subproblem and then integrates it with the upper level. This formulation allows the model to leverage the general structure from unlabeled data, the task-specific alignment from labeled speech, and the knowledge transfer from a teacher network within a single optimization loop. The experiments on LibriSpeech with a FastConformer backbone demonstrate that these strategies yield the consistent improvements over the conventional two-stage pre-training and fine-tuning pipeline, as well as over the prior bilevel optimization methods.

items.title: LLM-as-Joiner: Decoupling Alignment from Language Modeling in Label-synchronous ASR
items.authors: Jaeyoung Lee(NTT, Inc.; Kyoto University); Masato Mimura(NTT, Inc.); Ryo Magoshi(Kyoto University); Tatsuya Kawahara(Kyoto University)
items.abstract: We present LLM-as-Joiner, an LLM-based ASR architecture that decouples speech-text alignment from language modeling. A speech encoder first converts an input of T acoustic frames into U token-level speech states, one per output token, following the Aligner-Encoder framework. A pretrained LLM then predicts the transcript from these U states, with speech injected at a chosen LLM layer; only upper LLM layers are adapted via LoRA. Compared to conventional decoder-only speech-as-prefix decoding, the LLM operates on a shorter context (U rather than T + U), reducing memory and compute. On LibriSpeech and multilingual Common Voice, the proposed LLM-as-Joiner outperforms size-matched baselines, and joint training with a lightweight recognizer yields additional gains in the lightweight head, suggesting implicit transfer of linguistic knowledge from the LLM to the speech encoder.

items.title: Accurate Source-Free Speech Classification via Meta-Learned Target-Centric Model Merging
items.authors: Ka Hyun Park(Seoul National University); Junghun Kim(Seoul National University); U Kang(Seoul National University)
items.abstract: How can we build a speech classifier for an unseen domain when access to source-domain data is unavailable? Speech classification is widely used (e.g., voice commands, emotion recognition, etc.), but it is highly sensitive to domain shifts (e.g., languages), often causing substantial performance degradation. This issue becomes critical when source data cannot be accessed and only pretrained source models with limited target data are available. Under such constraints, typical adaptation approaches are inapplicable, and existing model merging methods easily overfit the limited target data. We propose Mᴏᴄʜᴇᴇ, an accurate target-centric model merging framework that combines multiple pretrained source models using limited target data. To improve generalization under scarce target labels, Mᴏᴄʜᴇᴇ exploits meta-learning to resolve representation misalignment and emphasize target-relevant sources. Extensive experiments show that Mᴏᴄʜᴇᴇ outperforms the baselines by up to 14.5 points in Macro-F1.

title: Code-Switching ASR
header: Thursday 1 October 2026 - 09:00-11:00 - Area 9 - Oral 2 - Code-Switching ASR

items.title: LLM-HB: Language-Aware LLM-Guided Hotword Biasing for Code-Switching ASR
items.authors: Yuxuan He(Shanghai Jiao Tong University; iFLYTEK Company Limited; Wuhan University); Genshun Wan(iFLYTEK Company Limited); Pengcheng Li(iFLYTEK); Gongping Huang(Wuhan University); JianQing Gao(iFLYTEK); Yanmin Qian(Shanghai Jiao Tong University)
items.abstract: Code-switching (CS) speech, characterized by language alternation within a single utterance, is prevalent in multilingual communities and poses challenges to automatic speech recognition (ASR) due to rapid language transitions. We propose LLM-HB, a language-aware large language model-guided hotword biasing framework for code-switching ASR (CS-ASR). The framework incorporates a mixture-of-experts (MoE) adaptor and an auxiliary language prediction head to better capture and differentiate multilingual representations, while hotwords are injected through LLM-based prompting. Experiments on the ASRU2019 code-switching challenge test set demonstrate that LLM-HB achieves a 20.30% relative reduction in mixed error rate (MER) over the baseline, reaching 5.85% MER under a 15-distractor hotword setting. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to integrate LLM-guided biasing into code-switching ASR. We further release the extracted ASRU2019 hotword list to support future research.

items.title: Improving Code-Switching ASR with Code-Mixing Guided Synthetic Speech
items.authors: Yue Heng Yeo(NTU, Singapore; I2R ASTAR Singapore); Haoyang Li(NTU, Singapore); Yizhou Peng(NTU, Singapore); Shreyas Gopal(NTU, Singapore); Hexin Liu(NTU, Singapore); Leibny Paola Garcia-Perera(Johns Hopkins University, USA); Hardik B. Sailor(I2R ASTAR Singapore); Jeremy H. M. Wong(Google DeepMind, Singapore); Eng Siong Chng(NTU, Singapore)
items.abstract: Code-switch (CS) Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) remains challenging due to limited availability of high quality CS text-speech pairs for training. Although synthetic data augmentation via text-to-speech (TTS) has been explored, existing CS TTS approaches primarily optimise reconstruction fidelity and do not explicitly enforce language-boundary consistency, thereby limiting their effectiveness for CS ASR augmentation. This paper proposes a code-mixing guided preference-learning framework that steers synthetic speech generation toward improved code-switching fidelity using the Code Mixing Index (CMI). Experiments on the SEAME Mandarin-English conversational corpus demonstrate that the proposed method enhances the utility of synthetic data for ASR fine-tuning. Specifically, when fine-tuning Whisper Large, the proposed approach reduces Mixed Error Rate (MER) from 12.1%/17.8% to 8.9%/14.2% on the DevMAN and DevSGE sets, respectively.

items.title: Reinforcement Learning for Data-Efficient Code-Switched ASR
items.authors: Ziwei Ye(Independent Researcher); Peter Vickers(Spotify Canada)
items.abstract: Audio-language models can be prompted for code-switched speech, but their decoding is not optimized for code-switching and often fails at language boundaries. We propose a practical reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards recipe for data-efficient adaptation of audio-language models to code-switched ASR using group relative policy optimization, combining an error rate reward with a script fidelity reward that penalizes wrong writing systems and a two-pass draft-and-refinement procedure. Using Qwen2-Audio as a reproducible testbed across 10 language pairs, training on only TTS code-switched speech, we show that RLVR with 10% of the data matches LoRA supervised fine-tuning trained on the full dataset, with the largest gains on typologically distant pairs. The error rate reward eliminates translation errors while the script fidelity reward separately reduces script contamination without degradation. These gains transfer zero-shot to a human-recorded code-switching corpus.

items.title: Direct Preference Optimization for English-Mandarin Code-Switching Speech Recognition in Audio LLMs
items.authors: Trung Nguyen(Institue of Infocomm Research, A*STAR; Nanyang Technological University); Cheng Yi Lewis Won(Institue of Infocomm Research, A*STAR); Minh Duc Pham(Institue of Infocomm Research, A*STAR); Yingxu He(Institue of Infocomm Research, A*STAR); Shuo Sun(Institue of Infocomm Research, A*STAR); Ai Ti Aw(Institue of Infocomm Research, A*STAR)
items.abstract: Audio large language models (Audio LLMs) exhibit systematic failures in transcribing code-switching speech despite strong multilingual capabilities. Focusing on English-Mandarin, we identify three failure modes: language omission, translation-instead-of-transcription, and hallucination. We apply Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) to align models, constructing preference pairs in which chosen responses preserve mixed-language content while rejected responses mimic failure patterns. Training three Audio LLMs on 100K pairs (570 hours), we observe consistent behavioral shifts: models learn to preserve language composition rather than translating when prompted for transcription. This alignment yields MER reductions up to 89.6% (in-distribution) and 20.0% (out-of-distribution). Our findings suggest DPO can effectively elicit correct code-switching transcription behavior from multilingual Audio LLMs.

items.title: Adding Robust Code-Switching Capabilities to High Performance Multilingual ASR
items.authors: Enes Yavuz Ugan(KIT); Alexander Waibel(KIT; CMU)
items.abstract: Code-switching (CSW) remains challenging for large multilingual ASR systems in real-world deployment. While fine-tuning on synthetic CSW data is possible, it generally degrades strong monolingual baselines. Our goal is to preserve these capabilities while extending models to handle complex code-switching, including morphological variations across languages. We propose Bayesian factorized adaptation, which learns to efficiently integrate switching-relevant knowledge into strong pretrained models without overwriting existing capabilities. Requiring only a small amount of synthetic data, our approach reduces transcription errors by 32.87% on code-switched words while improving overall WER by 5.31%, all while maintaining monolingual performance. Our results demonstrate that effective CSW adaptation depends more on knowledge integration than data complexity.

items.title: Dynamic Block-Online Streaming ASR for Low-Resource Agglutinative Code-Switching Speech with Morphology-Aware Evaluation
items.authors: Kazi Rafat(North South University); Afifa Imran(Apurba NSU R&D Lab); Md. Ismail Hossain(Apurba NSU R&D Lab); Md. Romzan Ali(Apurba NSU R&D Lab); Fuad Rahman(Apurba Technologies); Sifat Momen(Apurba NSU R&D Lab); Shafin Rahman(Apurba NSU R&D Lab); Nabeel Mohammed(Apurba NSU R&D Lab)
items.abstract: Low-resource, agglutinative languages challenge low-latency ASR, as fixed lookahead windows fail when grapheme order diverges, suffixes cross code-switch boundaries, or code-switching data is imbalanced. We present the first comprehensive study of streaming ASR for intra-sentential Bangla-English code-switching, identifying a mismatch between strict causal streaming and long-range morphological dependencies. We introduce a Dynamic Block-Online framework with VAD-aligned inference that balances semantics, latency, and context, enabling global bidirectional attention to preserve morphological integrity. To mitigate data scarcity, we propose Script-Anchored Loanword Injection, augmenting training text with English loanwords to model phonotactic transitions. We introduce CS-WER to diagnose switch, root, and suffix errors, and show that flexible latency budgets enhance recognition of agglutinative and mixed-language speech, with successful transfer to menstrual-medical domains.

title: Information Extraction and Retrieval / Survey Talk
header: Thursday 1 October 2026 - 09:00-11:00 - Area 12 - Oral 4 - Information Extraction and Retrieval / Survey Talk

items.title: Expressive Speech Translation
items.abstract: Speech to speech translation is still a challenging problem, without much consensus about model architectures, training data, evaluation methods, and so on. One frontier in this area is the preservation of the expressiveness of the input speech in the translation. Expressiveness ranges from global properties such as the speaker's voice and emotion as well as acoustic conditions, to local properties such as pauses, varying speaking rates, emphasis, and pitch for individual words. This survey will cover various aspects, such as training data, data synthesis methods, speech representation, model architectures, the use of large language models, and evaluation metrics.

items.title: Personalized Keyword Spotting for User-Defined Keywords Leveraging Text-Independent Speaker Verification
items.authors: Ming-Hsiang Hu(National Taiwan Normal University); Kuan-Tang Huang(National Taiwan Normal University); Chien-Chun Wang(E.SUN Financial Holding Co., Ltd.); Hung-Shin Lee(United Link Co., Ltd.); Berlin Chen(National Taiwan Normal University)
items.abstract: User-defined keyword spotting (UD-KWS) enables zero-shot wake-word detection from text, but existing systems learn speaker-invariant representations that cannot reject impostors uttering the correct keyword. We address this dual zero-shot setting—unseen keywords and unseen speakers—with ZP-KWS, a lightweight framework combining a phoneme-supervised audio encoder with a GE2E-pretrained compact speaker encoder (about 0.9M parameters). Multiplicative late fusion at inference grants each branch independent veto power, supporting modes from conventional detection to strict speaker-gated activation without retraining. On LibriPhrase, Google Speech Commands, and Qualcomm datasets, ZP-KWS reduces target-only FRR at 1% FAR by up to 60% relative to the strongest baseline while maintaining competitive keyword detection, all within a 1.55M parameter budget for edge deployment.

items.title: wav2tok 2.0: Scalable Audio Tokenization Maintaining Explicit Pairwise Token Alignment for Efficient Audio Retrieval
items.authors: Adhiraj Banerjee(Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur); Vipul Arora(Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur; KU Leuven)
items.abstract: Learning discrete speech representations that preserve similarity across variable-length utterances is central to query-by-example spoken term detection (QbE-STD). While wav2tok introduced CTC-based sequence alignment to enforce token consistency, its tightly coupled clustering and alignment training recipe limits scalability. We propose wav2tok 2.0, a scalable alignment-aware speech tokenizer built on the BEST-STD backbone. wav2tok 2.0 employs staged training, first learning discriminative, speaker-invariant representations via contrastive learning and vector quantization, and then enforcing pairwise token consistency using a CTC alignment loss and a novel DTW-aligned framewise prediction objective with adaptive weighting. Experiments show that wav2tok 2.0 consistently outperforms BEST-STD and general-purpose tokenizers on QbE-STD while remaining efficient and scalable.

items.title: Rethinking Organization Entity Modeling in End-to-End Acoustic Named Entity Recognition
items.authors: Spandan Dey(Samsung R&D Institute India-Bangalore); Nidhi Mantri(Samsung R&D Institute India-Bangalore); Sambit Behera(Samsung R&D Institute India-Bangalore); Hirak Mondal(Samsung R&D Institute India-Bangalore); Sanjay Kurmi(Samsung R&D Institute India-Bangalore); Sreyasree Mandal(Samsung R&D Institute India-Bangalore); Atharv Joshi(Samsung R&D Institute India-Bangalore); Premjeet Singh(Samsung R&D Institute India-Bangalore); Gopal Agrawal(Samsung R&D Institute India-Bangalore)
items.abstract: End-to-end acoustic named entity recognition (NER) integrates speech transcription and entity detection within a unified model, avoiding error propagation in cascaded ASR-NER systems. However, organization entities remain significantly harder to detect due to multi-word spans, acronyms, and lexical variability. We present a systematic analysis of organization recognition failures in acoustic NER, revealing that conventional cross-entropy training inadequately models entity span dependencies. To address this limitation, we propose an organization-aware Whisper-based acoustic NER framework combining LLM-based targeted semantic augmentation, category-specific boundary supervision, and a structure-constrained entity learning (SCEL) objective that enforces entity span consistency during decoding. Experiments demonstrate substantial improvements in organization recognition while maintaining strong ASR performance, outperforming in entity-recognition for several other existing approaches.

items.title: AnySimLite: A Lightweight Few-Shot Similarity Encoder for On-Device Speech-Adjacent Classification
items.authors: Sourav Ghosh(Samsung R&D Institute Bangalore); Yash Bhatia(Samsung R&D Institute Bangalore); Keshav Goyal(Samsung R&D Institute Bangalore); Sahil Singh Bagri(Samsung R&D Institute Bangalore); Mohamed Akram Ulla Shariff(Samsung R&D Institute Bangalore); Saravana Balaji Shanmugam(Samsung R&D Institute Bangalore)
items.abstract: To minimize privacy concerns and inference latency on edge devices like smartphones, lightweight on-device models remain important for end-user applications. Many of these applications involve natural language classification, but deploying multiple specialized models creates a memory footprint challenge. We investigate: Can a single lightweight architecture solve multiple Speech-Adjacent (SA) classification tasks through reduction to a nuanced text similarity formulation? We propose ANYSIM-LITE, a lightweight similarity encoder that combines word-level and character-level channels. Together with a dataset transformation strategy, we evaluate ANYSIM-LITE across multiple SA classification tasks and show that it consistently achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) or SOTA-competitive performance in few-shot settings while maintaining a low memory footprint. Even in the worst case, the performance drop remains below 7% while using < 1/250th of the model size of the SOTA qLLaMA_LoRA-7B baseline.
