items.title: Personalized Electrolaryngeal Voice Conversion with a Single Pre-operative Utterance
items.authors: Devin Chang(Academia Sinica); Hsin-Te Hwang(Academia Sinica); Ming-Chi Yen(Academia Sinica; National Taiwan University); Shu-Wei Tsai(National Cheng Kung University Hospital); Yu Tsao(Academia Sinica); Hsin-Min Wang(Academia Sinica)
items.abstract: Electrolaryngeal voice conversion (ELVC) enhances the mechanical speech of laryngectomees to improve naturalness and intelligibility. While personalized ELVC typically requires extensive pre-operative recordings for supervised training, this paper investigates a one-shot scenario where only one natural utterance is available for timbre preservation. We evaluate two strategies using zero-shot VC models: (1) a cascaded approach, performing ELVC followed by secondary conversion to the target timbre; and (2) a pseudo-target strategy, using a zero-shot model to generate synthetic training data for a supervised ELVC model. Results indicate that the cascaded approach outperforms the pseudo-target strategy, remarkably improving speaker similarity and quality with minimal impact on intelligibility. We also demonstrate that direct application of zero-shot models to ELVC fails due to domain mismatch, confirming the necessity of our proposed framework for one-shot personalized voice restoration.

items.title: A Preclinical Study of Electrolaryngeal Voice Conversion for a Novel Nasal Electrolarynx: Feature Choice and Data Augmentation
items.authors: Qi-Yan Chen(Academia Sinica); Ming-Chi Yen(Academia Sinica; National Taiwan University); Fo-Rui Li(National Central University); Hsin-Te Hwang(Academia Sinica); Ching-Hung Lai(National Cheng Kung University Hospital); Shu-Wei Tsai(National Cheng Kung University Hospital); Ping-Cheng Yeh(National Taiwan University); Jyh-Shing Roger Jang(National Taiwan University); Yu Tsao(Academia Sinica); Hsin-Min Wang(Academia Sinica)
items.abstract: Electrolaryngeal (EL) speech often exhibits reduced intelligibility and naturalness due to imperfect excitation and fixed pitch. In this preclinical study, we present the first systematic investigation of electrolaryngeal voice conversion (ELVC) for speech produced by a newly invented nasal electrolarynx (NEL), extending previous work that mainly targets cervical EL (CEL) speech. We examine the choice of features under NEL's distinctive acoustics by comparing Mel-spectrograms and WavLM features as input to a seq2seq ELVC system. To address NEL data scarcity, we propose an LLE-VC-based augmentation strategy to synthesize paired sNEL--sNL speech for VC pretraining. Experiments reveal device-dependent trends: WavLM features benefit CEL-oriented conversion and augmentation, whereas Mel-spectrogram inputs better preserve NEL-specific spectral characteristics and yield better intelligibility-related metrics and listener preferences for NEL-to-NL conversion.

items.title: One-to-Many Electrolaryngeal Voice Conversion with Synthetic Data
items.authors: Bowen Wu(RIKEN; ATR); Haruto Ueno(RIKEN; The University of Osaka); Carlos Toshinori Ishi(RIKEN; ATR); Chaoran Liu(RIKEN; ATR; NII)
items.abstract: Restoring natural (NL) speech from electrolarynx (EL) speech is crucial for EL users who have undergone laryngectomy. While previous works have shown the effectiveness of deep learning methods for converting EL-to-NL speech with data augmentation, time-aligned conversion remains underexplored, where data scarcity is more severe due to temporal constraints. We propose a data-driven learning framework to learn from small-scale (13 minutes) EL speech data to synthesize time-aligned EL speech from NL speech of multiple speakers, for developing one-to-many EL-to-NL conversion models. Our method leverages pretrained deep learning-based any-to-many voice conversion (VC) models for finetuning on EL speech for NL-to-EL conversion, to convert the NL speech in a large-scale multi-speaker corpus to synthetic EL speech, which is used to supervise a pretrained VC model for one-to-many EL-to-NL VC. Experiments show the effectiveness of our method against baselines in intonation and intelligibility.

items.title: Tongue2Speech: Real-Time Speech Synthesis from Tongue Ultrasound Videos via Spatiotemporal Transformers
items.authors: Yash Sonkar(IIIT Hyderabad); Yasaswi Kilaru(IIIT Hyderabad); Sudheera Yelimeli(IIIT Hyderabad); Neil Shah(IIIT Hyderabad; TCS Research); Vineet Gandhi(IIIT Hyderabad)
items.abstract: Ultrasound-to-Speech aims to synthesize intelligible speech from tongue ultrasound video. Prior approaches rely mainly on purely convolutional or recurrent architectures. We present Tongue2Speech, a lightweight framework combining explicit 3D spatio-temporal encoding with a multi-layer Transformer to model long-range articulatory dynamics. Spectral distortion metrics (such as MSE) commonly used in prior work are weak indicators of lexical accuracy when used in isolation. Therefore, we evaluate performance using word error rate (WER). On the English TaL corpus, Tongue2Speech achieves 15.93% WER in single-speaker and 31.64% in multi-speaker settings, outperforming six strong baselines. Speaker-specific fine-tuning further improves intelligibility for unseen users. These results highlight tongue-only ultrasound as a promising pathway toward practical silent speech synthesis. Audio samples are available at: https://tongue2speech.github.io/

items.title: On the Role of the Tongue Region in Ultrasound-to-Acoustic Mapping
items.authors: Ibrahim Ibrahimov(Department of TelecommBudapest University of Technology and Economics); Gábor Gosztolya(HUN-REN–SZTE Research Group on Artificial Intelligence; University of Szeged); Csaba Zainkó(Budapest University of Technology and Economics)
items.abstract: Ultrasound tongue imaging is a promising modality for Silent Speech Interfaces, yet a core assumption in ultrasound-to-acoustic mapping remains untested, namely that the tongue is the primary source of acoustic information. We test this hypothesis by proposing an automatic tongue region extraction method for controlled input manipulation on a 2D-CNN baseline, and a dual encoder with cross-attention gating for mapping ultrasound frames to 80-dimensional mel-spectrograms. Based on our results, surprisingly, removing the tongue region produced no statistically significant MSE degradation, suggesting the 2D-CNN may exploit broader image cues rather than tongue-specific features. The dual encoder similarly yields no significant gain over the baseline across MSE, MCD, PESQ, and MOSnet. However, Grad-CAM maps reveal that the dual encoder focuses activations on the tongue region, unlike the baseline, representing a meaningful step towards more interpretable ultrasound-to-acoustic mapping.

items.title: Low-Burden Data Augmentation for Dysarthric ASR via Zero-Shot Voice Cloning
items.authors: Satwinder Singh(University of Auckland); Qianli Wang(University of Auckland); Zihan Zhong(University of Auckland); Clarion Mendes(University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign); Mark Hasegawa-Johnson(University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign); Waleed Abdulla(University of Auckland); Seyed Reza Shahamiri(University of Auckland)
items.abstract: Automatic speech recognition remains unreliable for dysarthric speech due to data scarcity and high inter-speaker variability. While synthetic data can address these gaps, traditional methods often require extensive speaker-specific data, reintroducing the collection bottleneck. We investigate zero-shot voice cloning as a low-burden augmentation strategy, using Higgs Audio V2 to clone speakers in the TORGO dataset. We fine-tune (FT) Whisper-medium on cloned, real, and hybrid data and evaluate on held-out real speech. Compared to the zero-shot (31.62%), Clone FT achieved a competitive 26.00% WER, nearly matching the 24.44% and 25.12% seen with Real and Hybrid FT, respectively. Notably, Clone and Hybrid FT outperform Real FT for moderate-severe speakers. Clone FT achieves the best results (11.45% relative) in cross-corpus evaluation on the SAP-1102. These results suggest that zero-shot cloning provides scalable training data that circumvents the costly data collection bottleneck.
